Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order regarding a set of serious concerns I have about the vote yesterday evening on concurrence at the report stage of Bill C-44, the Hibernia development project bill.
I have reviewed the tapes and have reviewed Hansard for that moment, and I would like to bring the following to the House's attention.
Yesterday, when the Deputy Speaker put the question, I and other members of my caucus said no. The Chair did not hear us, and I assume that others around her did not either, or they would have advised her of the dissenting voices. However, Mr. Speaker, we did not say no. I can only assume that our dissent to this bill was drowned out by the collective voices of the Liberals and Conservatives who were much closer to the Speaker than ourselves.
The result of this inability to hear was that our caucus was unable to vote against this stage of the bill. Yet, we have spoken repeatedly against this project at second reading, during report stage debate and debate on the time allocation motion. Surely the House should have anticipated that a bill which required time allocation would not be adopted unanimously.
This is not the first time that the House has encountered difficulties on important divisions, but I would like to think that this will be the last.
I seek your guidance, Mr. Speaker, on finding means to ensure that our voices are heard by the Chair in the
future. In the meantime, however, the record shows that concurrence at report stage was given unanimously. This is clearly an incorrect record. I would like that division to be taken again but understand of course that the Chair and the House would be reluctant to do so.
At the very least, I would like to move that the record be corrected to show that concurrence was not given unanimously. I have an appropriate motion which I think will indicate very simply that. I would like to read the motion and then seek unanimous consent to have it put. I move:
That the record of debate at report stage of Bill C-44, an act respecting the Hibernia development project and to amend certain acts in relation thereto, be amended by deleting the words ''Accordingly, the bill, as amended, was concurred in at report stage" and replacing them with the following: "Accordingly, the bill, as amended, was concurred in at report stage, on division".
I would like to seek unanimous consent to be able to put that motion. That would then not change what happened yesterday. Of course a decision was made. I think that inadvertently, because of the rather exuberant mood of the House at that moment, the noes that were stated at that time simply were not heard by the Speaker.
If the House were to accept this motion, it would simply clear the record, and we would be able to move on with the business of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last April 27, 1989, the first thing in the morning that day, the Minister of Finance rose on a question of privilege concerning the leak in his budget that had occurred the previous evening. Hon. members will recall the events of that day. We now have had extensive coverage of those events in the press.
I gave Your Honour notice of my intention to raise this question a week ago Monday. I waited until today to allow the government some time to prepare its response and for us to deal with the issue in a non-urgent way because of course I think the urgency is gone, but I think it is an important question that was not dealt with on April 27.
I want to raise it again because of the fact that the court cases that were involved following that leak are now completed. The matter is no longer sub judice. Accordingly, we can deal with it in this House.
Hon. members will recall the sequence of events. In fact we now know there were two leaks of this budget that occurred on or about April 24, 1989. The minister became aware of one of those leaks, as did the whole country, on April 26 when Mr. Small appeared on television brandishing his copy of The Budget in Brief.
The Minister of Finance came into the House and through the Minister of Justice tried to get the House to sit late that evening. There was no agreement to do so. The minister released his budget on national television, and then the next day the question of privilege was raised by the Minister of Finance.
I notice that in the minister's question of privilege, which was the first one raised that day-and Your Honour indicated that you had received notice of many-there was no request by the minister for any reference to a committee of the circumstances surrounding the budget leak or anything to do with it.
Indeed, I do not know exactly what the minister's question of privilege was. He gave Your Honour notice of one, but he did not actually come out with anything that indicated a breach of his privileges.
I submit that while he may have been embarrassed by the leak, I do not think that he personally suffered a breach of privilege any more than the rest of us did, but the rest of us did suffer subsequent ones: one because the budget was dealt with outside this House, which I will come back to in a moment, but also the subsequent conduct of the Minister of Finance and the other ministers who spoke on April 27. In my view this prejudiced the opposition members of Parliament and thereby deprived us of privileges that we might otherwise have enjoyed.

Since Mr. Small is charged, specifically, only with possession, his conduct in disclosing the contents of the budget on a telecast is not an issue before this court. Some might argue, for instance, that he could have fulfilled his journalistic obligations by revealing only the fact that budgetary secrecy had been breached, without revealing the details and contents of the document. Whether such bare-fact disclosure, without details, would have carried the credibility and impact appropriate to such a serious problem is doubtful. A society that recognizes the importance to the democratic process, of the free dissemination of news, should not be offended if that dissemination takes place with the measure of dramatic flair demonstrated by Mr. Small. Notwithstanding Professor McLuhan's observation, sometimes message overcomes medium. Indeed, Small's revelations on television and the resultant immediate response by the Minister of Finance, may well be viewed as having forestalled any real mischief with regard to the "Mutual Life" leak. Staff Sergeant Jordan raised this speculation early in his deliberations. Mr. Small's conduct in his subsequent dealings with the law enforcement authorities appears 1o have been exemplary.

There is no legal canon prohibiting the application of common sense. Based upon all of the foregoing considerations, I find that abuse of process has been made out in this case on a balance of probabilities. Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present the fourth report of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General, on prostitution and soliciting.
This is a short report which is a review of the legislation which was in effect. As we know, in most cities, the legislation was working well. However, in Toronto and Vancouver, it was not working quite so well. We have made only three recommendations.
We have also noted, since the prostitutes are usually victims of social injustice, child abuse, and so on, that they should not be further punished. We have recommended that social programs be set up to allow them to conduct a safer life-style.
We have made some recommendations because the police did want to identify these people and we have recommended changes to the Identification of Criminals Act.
I would like to table this report.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
that Bill C-44, an act respecting the Hibernia Development Project and to amend acts in relation thereto, be read the third time and passed.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am delighted to be addressing the House today on the occasion of third reading of Bill C-44, the Hibernia Development Project Act.
As I have had occasion to do previously in this House, I want to thank members both from my party and members opposite who have debated this bill but who have always supported the development of Hibernia.
They have supported it possibly for reasons the government proposed or possibly for additional reasons, and while the emphasis from time to time might have been different on the two sides, the bottom line on Hibernia has been co-operation. There has been a serious attempt within this House to examine carefully what is the best

October 4, 1990
Government Orders
arrangement on the Hibernia project. Today, they have come together to work for the completion of this project. I thank them for that.
The Hibernia project goes back a long way. Some people who possibly saw the first activity on the Grand Banks have become not old men and women, but definitely people more experienced and in some cases possibly even cynical. I would suggest that this act today within this House will remove another portion, another facet, of the cynicism which I believe began to erode as we were able to sign the agreement in Newfoundland September 14 last.
It has been an eventful 10 days, and possibly something happened here that does not happen too often in this House. I want to go on public record to thank members of the Public Service, both from the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador.
As well, I thank the advisers of the companies that form the consortium. They have worked not hours, not days, not weeks, not even months, but literally years on this process. They worked not only from a professional point of view but also from a mandate that they were given from the different parties, relative to the agreements relating to Hibernia. They worked, I believe, in the best interests of our country. So it has been an eventful time.
I know this summer, even though it slipped by for most of us, the fact of the matter is that I saw men and women giving up much of their time, quite apart from the professionalism which we expect from them, to get this work done.
What has happened is that the bill, which was introduced last November, has had a very detailed process both in this House and in the negotiations which culminated in the signing of the document escrow and closing agreements on September 14. This event has locked in the business deal and is only subject to final approval by Parliament.
As has been noted, many of us had the pleasure of participating in the signing ceremony in St. John's together with a number of my federal colleagues, officials from the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador and members of the Hibernia consortium.
I also want to thank the Prime Minister. I do not do this only because he is Prime Minister or because he is my political leader. Many members in this House will know that in the post June 24 period there was much debate in our country as to what would be the state of federal-provincial relations.
Despite the rumours I would read in the newspapers or the commentary that I would see on television or hear on radio, the Prime Minister throughout that summer gave me, this process and this project not only his total support but also always kept his eye on the purpose of the Hibernia project. He described it himself when he said: "This is more than oil or barrels of oil. This relates to fairness and to dignity."
Hopefully, in some tangible measure, the Hibernia project will bring that not only to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador but to Canadians generally.
I do not want to be one of those politicians who, from time to time is accused of overstating the case, but I believe this event, this project, marks a major breakthrough for Canada's petroleum industry.
The Hibernia development project will contribute to the ongoing diversification of Canada's energy supply sources. The effects of this development will also be long lasting, not only for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, but for Canadians across the nation. We believe that Hibernia is only the first step in building the new skills, the expertise, and technology required to meet the challenges of frontier development.
I had occasion this summer to meet with some of the men who worked at the first oil well in Leduc, or what is known as Leduc No. 1, back in the last part of the 1940s, 1947-48. I am reminded of one particular gentleman, a farm boy from Saskatchewan in those days, who worked at Leduc. This gentleman told me about what happened on those days.
He told me, for example, that the night before Leduc was to come in, there were farmers and people from around the whole area along what are called section roads in the west, waiting for the events of the next day. He told me, as if it had happened yesterday, what Leduc No. 1 meant, not only to him personally, but to Alberta at that time.
October 4, 1990

We should remind ourselves that Alberta at one time had to come cap in hand to the government of Canada for help, and how today the province of Alberta benefits all of us not only by a secure oil supply-and we only have to take a look at events in the Persian Gulf to be reminded of that-but also Albertans have been contributing to equalization and the well-being of all Canadians for many, many years, partly because of the hard work of some people who possibly did not know what they were building back in the latter part of the 1940s.
He told me, for example, of the next wells that came in, the gushers and the problems they had from a technological point of view. He told me how they had to dig ponds to trap oil they had hit and which they did not know how to handle. In one area they recovered approximately one and a half million barrels hat way, literally by oil flowing down trenches into holding ponds.
That sounds primitive today, but it was real. It was from these humble beginnings that an oil industry was developed which today in world standards is seen as one of the very best.
I do not think that Canadians who really look at Hibernia and the risks that any of these large projects mean for all of us, that the risks of Hibernia in today's context are much different from what happened in Alberta in the latter 1940s.
I look at places like Stevanger in Norway and see what happened in that community in terms of servicing the offshore oil industry in the North Sea, or what happened in northern England or Scotland and the technology they developed. Too often as Canadians we take for granted for instance what the Dutch, or the Norwegians or some of the Pacific nations have been able to learn from these kinds of projects and that we as Canadians somehow will be left out.
I believe that Hibernia can be for all of us as Canadians that next frontier. I sincerely believe that. I do not think I have overstated the case. I would hope that for all of us that is what Hibernia will mean.
I spend a fair bit of my time time in Alberta because of my responsibilities. I have been meeting people time after time who have said to me: "Make Hibernia go". We want to see it completed because we believe it is going to help the energy industry of Canada. I thank them for that viewpoint as well in respect to this project.
Government Orders
While we will get some new skills, expertise, technologies from other countries obviously, we should not ever have the view that we have all the ideas. But we want to develop them for ourselves as well. I look forward to Hibernia doing that. We will develop engineering experience in the offshore that we should be able to market in other parts of the world. These are the kinds of spin-offs that we as a country have to examine.
Although the binding agreements have been finalized, they are being held in escrow by an independent third party until one remaining hurdle is cleared. That brings us to our task at hand today, the passage of Bill C-44.
Members of this government, along with many of our colleagues on the other side of the House, are very anxious to finalize this enabling legislation. There has been much debate over the matter of federal participation in the Hibernia project. It has been clear for some time that the Hibernia project is simply too costly and massive an undertaking to proceed without public support. In recognition of this in 1988 we joined the Government of Newfoundland and five private sector firms in signing a statement of principles to develop Hibernia. Bill C-44 will authorize the government to enter into legally binding agreements to fulfil its commitments made in the statement of principles.
This is also not unique. There is criticism from time to time about the so-called megaprojects but energy, generally speaking, is a megaproject. It is its very nature and while, yes, there has to be emphasis on smaller electrical projects-and I will be coming forward with programs on that later this year-I remind members that today as we look at the world around us, that because of oil and its development, we for example do not face the realities of our neighbour to the south who is now looking at importing 50 per cent of its oil and gas supplies. Surely with the long lead times it behoves us to move forward on these projects.
When Suncor came onstream did it make a lot of sense? One might have questioned the economics of it. Syncrude made more sense. I remember in 1979 , as Indian affairs minister, we were working on the Cold Lake project because there were a lot of native people involved. It makes sense today. Surely the frontier is a blessing, an opportunity that has been given to us as Canadians. We have not done anything to deserve it, nor have we done anything to put it there. It is our responsibility to use these resources not only for our benefit but for the larger community.

October 4, 1990
Government Orders
I want to explain the federal government's, that is the taxpayers' involvement, in this project and why we did it. More than $5 billion Canadian will be spent bringing Hibernia into production. Approximately $3 billion will be spent in Canada, including $1.6 billion for work to be done in the province of Newfoundland. In addition to the $5.2 billion in capital spending needed to bring Hibernia to production there will be a further $3.5 billion expenditure over the life of the project. This project, while extremely important for the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, is obviously a project that has national importance.
As was outlined in the statement of principles, the Government of Canada will provide the consortium with a cash contribution for 25 per cent of eligible pre-production capital costs up to a maximum of $1.04 billion. We will also guarantee loans for 40 per cent of those costs to a maximum of $1.66 billion. I want to tell hon. members that that is-and I want to use the word very specifically-a loan.
Yes, we could have gone the other way. We could have made it a Government of Canada and Government of Newfoundland project, but I hear criticism around this place that we should have done it all at the taxpayers' money. Then I imagine the governments would have been accused of exposing ourselves to too much risk. The risk is $5.2 billion then.
I ask members to look at this project very carefully, the loan, the provision we built into Hibernia on the lender risk sharing, as well as the pay-back depending on the price of oil. Surely members have to be realistic about whatever the price of oil will be when oil comes on in 1996 and then consider the period of time of the life of the field. It will have to be determined at that period of time what the return on investment is going to be, the ROI.
I ask members opposite if any one of us starts a business today can he or she guarantee for me 20 years hence what the return will be? Obviously there is a matter of financial return that we try to look at very carefully and the need to bring on a new source of supply. One always has to balance those two issues.
There has been some confusion in the press as to the true cost of the federal loan guarantees. Let me emphasize that the guarantees are a back stop, to be drawn upon only if the project revenue is insufficient to repay the debt. I can assure the House that the government will not agree to have provided these guarantees if it had any concern about the ability of the project to repay those loans.
Benefits emanating from the development of Hibernia for all Canadians are going to be substantial. Hibernia will play an important role in enhancing Canada's oil supply. I will comment further on that in a moment.
The project establishes a new frontier for Canada. It will diversify Canada's oil supply and offset the expected decline in conventional light oil production from western Canada. With the production of 110,000 barrels per day, Hibernia will account for approximately 12 per cent of Canada's light oil production by the year 2000.
Very often Canadians forget the matter also of the type of oil we are going to get. I am concerned about the reduction or decline of the light oil production in the western sedimentary basin. What are those reserves? That is why we have to move into in situ oil, for example. That is why we need the Lloydminster upgrader and use the heavy oils, even with the differentials in price. That is why we have to seriously look at how to plan the next projects relating to the oil sands and what are our projects for northern Canada. These are our opportunities because these are resources given to Canadians, I say, by a divine hand.
Out of this comes another question. People say: "Well, yes, you are going to get the 110,000 barrels, but it is all going to go to the United States". That is an interesting concept because the 110,000 barrels will be bid on and, most likely at this present point in time, they would go to the United States.
There is an issue relating to how much to change refining capacity to refine that oil because of its heavy waxing quality. Are we better off for example to get other oil, offsetting this 110,000 barrels with offshore oil which we get through Portland, Maine and which we send to various refineries in eastern Canada up to Montreal?

Those are the types of questions which I think logic drives one to examine from the best economic position one can get.
I also hear from certain refiners in eastern Canada that with some modification obviously they will have to look at it from a financial point of view. There might be in an opportunity to bid on Hibernia oil. I would suggest that the marketplace is the best place to examine that issue.
The same thing could be said about Cohasset-Panuke, which I personally hope will come into being before the end of this mandate of this government. It is a light distillate. There is tremendous interest in that type of product. Even though that is a relatively small project by international standards or even Canadian standards, how best do we develop that resource so that the people of Nova Scotia will get some benefits and through that benefit the people of Canada?
The Hibernia project will dramatically bolster Newfoundland's economy. We saw a bit of that even when we had a reception. I imagine there was even some bolstering of the hospitality economy in Newfoundland during that day. I dare say that possibly that activity has even continued beyond the time I was there.
My good friend opposite talks about people ready to work building a road into Great Mosquito Cove. I hear complaints of people who say: "I want to work. Will I get hired?". So often around here we look at the large issues. What we sometimes have to do is step back and look at what is happening in the bush. What is happening in the muskeg? What is happening at the coast? What is happening to people? That is why I am excited about Hibernia.
Every dollar invested in this project will yield several dollars in primary and secondary benefits to Newfoundland. It is estimated that approximately 10,000 person-years of work will be created in Newfoundland during the construction phase. Perhaps even more important, over the long term new technical skills will be developed in the province's workforce, as well as that of other provinces, that will position us to take advantage of future offshore development in other areas of Canada.
Government Orders
Yes, I believe that Hibernia will rank in terms of names and recognition with places like Leduc. People will come to know Terra Nova, Ben Nevis, and Cohasset-Panuke. This is Canada. This is our opportunity. I am pleased that so many members opposite recognize these facts and with the strong support I have had from my own caucus.
In early 1989 the Hibernia consortium undertook to redesign the top side facilities of the project. The main support frame was eliminated. The number of modules was reduced from 20 smaller units to five supermodules. As a result of this redesign, the industrial benefits provisions outlined in the statement of principles were renegotiated in a way that will provide significant benefits for all of Canada.
The agreement goes beyond the statement of principles as a result of the consortium's commitment to undertake an additional two million person-hours of metal fabrication work in Canada. These new commitments are approximately to two supermodules, and this should be kept in mind.
I say to hon. members that as they evaluate this project for the last time in this House they should remember that the governments pursued a regional benefits objective package for Newfoundland and Labrador and wanted it expanded not only to that province but to the larger Canadian communities.
As a consequence the Hibernia consortium has agreed to fabricate one of the supermodules in Newfoundland and will use its best efforts to build a second supermodule in Canada.
What is the effect of all of this? The impact of Hibernia on the province, as we said, will be substantial. However, I remind members that when the first projects in the North Sea came into being-and nobody today questions North Sea-the people of Norway and the United Kingdom realized approximately 35 per cent of the expenditure for domestic placing of contracts within those two countries. It was about 35 per cent.
In the statement of principles we were shooting for Canadian content in the area of 45 per cent. With the changes in the negotiations which are now incorporated in this bill and the agreements we have in escrow right now, it will be in the area of 55 per cent to 60 per cent.

October 4, 1990
Government Orders
I believe that Canadians will deliver. Time after time I hear in this Elouse questioning: "Can we do it"? We have done it before. The oil industry has shown it can do it and it will do it again. We will do it with Hibernia as well.
Those are the facts. As a result, in every region of our country plants and industries are poised to meet the engineering and construction demands which will flow from the project.
Let me be very practical. This summer in my own backyard there was a looping of the trans-Canada pipeline. That is not very important, I imagine, in terms of larger Canadian energy projects and in terms of the length of time spent on the work they were doing. However, it was important because not only did it bring us new capacity which we so desperately need if we are going to move gas out of the gas fields but it had impact in the Manitoba economy.
Fellows got into their half-ton trucks at four o'clock in the morning and drove 80 miles to work. They were not concerned about the 80 miles. They were not even concerned about four o'clock. They wanted to go to work. These were farm fellows and people from the urban community.
Economic activity driven this way works. Canadians have always responded. If I can be very personal, my first exposure to this whole process was after I had graduated from high school and I was working for a car dealership in my home town. The trans-Canada pipeline was going through about 10 miles from our home town. At that time there were fellows there from Alberta and Saskatchewan and, granted, there were a lot of Oklahomans and Texans around. However, that was the year we sold more cars in that dealership than we had for many years before and would for many years after. Those are the practical impacts, the spinoffs.
I remind members-maybe there is even a chuckle or two-of what happens in this House with these some time almost prosaic kinds of discussions. Back home people know what this means.
Another point I want to mention concerns the environmental impact of energy production and energy transportation. I am aware of those impacts. I am committed, as is the industry, to ensuring that environmental considerations are integrated into the government's energy policy process. Environmental
assessments are a crucial component of the government's over-all evaluation of any energy project. All such projects are subjected to detailed environmental scrutiny and review designed to minimize potential adverse consequences.
The government has made it clear that projects will not proceed if they are not acceptable in environmental terms. The Hibernia project has undergone a rigorous environmental public review which provided an opportunity for all interested parties to voice their concerns and have those concerns addressed. Based on the review, the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board decided in 1986 that the Hibernia project could go ahead once the recommendations of the environmental assessment panel were adequately addressed. This requirement is being satisfied and at the same time my officials have assessed the environmental implications of the changes to the project design and the movement of the gravity base construction site to Trinity Bay.
I want to assure the House that the government is satisfied that all adverse environmental impacts have been addressed and, further, that all effects identified are insignificant or cannot be mitigated.
As I close, one point that I would like to emphasize is that it will give Canada and Canadians an unprecedented opportunity to develop a higher level of technical expertise in the development of the offshore energy source.
The design and construction of the Hibernia project will provide a wide array of important new business opportunities. These opportunities should be made available to Canadians. I know that the project will challenge the skills of Canadians and take them to the leading edge of technology.
Companies that meet the high standards demanded by Hibernia will be in a position to play an even larger role in future offshore projects in Canada and around the world. I find it exciting that through the joint initiative of two governments and the private sector, enormous economic benefits from Hibernia are now upon us.
I know this is a partisan place, but I want to say very clearly that for those of us who came from western Canada and even from a province like Manitoba where our production of oil is very small relative to Canadian production, when the western accord was signed, it was important for us because it was another plank in the long struggle for prairie provinces which, when we entered Confederation, had not been deemed worthy of ownership of our resources. That has been a long struggle.
October 4, 1990

It was a struggle which culminated in 1930 with the Natural Resources Transfer Act. There is still unfinished business in that bill. It relates to the satisfaction of Indians and claims that our native people have, which we in western Canada have to fulfil and complete.
Just as that was in my mind a step forward in bringing fairness to western Canada, who knows what would have happened had the Natural Resources Transfer Act of 1930 not taken place? Who knows?
The same thing applies to the Atlantic accord. I know my hon. friend opposite-and I want to end on this personal note-will understand when I speak of a man who came from Ireland, became a Canadian and was an institution in his own outport on the western coast of Newfoundland, the late Dr. Hugh Twomey.
Dr. Twomey was minister of health when I became-
He was a good Tory.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
He was a good Tory. They are all good Tories.
I remember when I met with the late Dr. Twomey as minister of health, we were discussing in September and October of 1984 how together we were going to implement the Canada Health Act.
As the hon. Speaker would know, there was some controversy about that act and how it might impact on the delivery of health services in the provinces.
I had visited the province of Nova Scotia in the morning, Prince Edward Island in the afternoon and Newfoundland in the evening. Then I wanted to return to Ottawa. There were a number of issues I wanted to discuss with the minister of health of the day.
I do not know what kind of a day he had had, but he did not want to discuss the Canada Health Act. He wanted to discuss everything else. Never have I heard more stories about Newfoundland and never did I have a better evening.
Government Orders
What I remember that evening-it was late by the time we left-Dr. Twomey got up. In the small gathering, he said: "Jake, you wanted to discuss the Canada Health Act. I did not want to, and that is rather evident."
But he said: "What I want to tell you is this: Go back to Ottawa. With the signing of the Atlantic accord, I believe sincerely that the people of Newfoundland and Labrador will not only make their living based on our traditional activities of fishing and making a living from the resources we have in place at the present time, that the Atlantic accord will give us an opportunity not only to develop the economy for our people, but also improve the conditions of their daily life."
He said: "I believe that just as things changed in Alberta, Hibernia can contribute to the development of our province. We will become not simply the recipients of equalization, but possibly some glorious day we will be in a position where we can pay other Canadians for the years of equalization that we received from them." He finished his little speech that evening with one statement which remained with me as we discussed Hibernia. He said simply this: "Mr. Minister, go back to Ottawa"-in this case it was the Canada Health Act-"and do for Newfoundland what you would do for other provinces and we will trust .you".
I believe that it was not my work; I was the recipient of the Atlantic accord. It was the vision of the Prime Minister to change a long history, a history based not only on changes that were needed, whether in one province or the other. In this case it happened to be Newfoundland's turn. I want to thank the Prime Minister for the vision and for the reality that this bill brings to us today.
Madam Speaker-

I would refer the hon. member to Standing Order 43 which says that the first

Government Orders
two speakers-the minister and the first member speaking in reply to the minister-have unlimited speaking time and that there are no questions or comments after their speeches. The hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception.

Madam Speaker, as the associate energy, mines and resources critic and as a Newfoundlander, indeed as a Canadian, and even as a Liberal member of Parliament, I am delighted to respond to the excellent presentation given by the hon. minister. It gives me an opportunity to put together a number of things that have been said in the House by members on both sides and both ends of the House, an opportunity really for the public perhaps to see the entire package as it started, some of the snags that we have had, some of the comments we have had in the House, some of the difficulties we are going to have in the future and perhaps some of the prognostications with respect to what this project may bring, mostly on the good side.
Incidentally, may I welcome you to the chair. It is nice to see you in the chair and I look forward to more times with you as the Assistant Deputy Speaker.
However, Mr. Speaker, to continue, and to put this in a perspective of time, when I first heard of what has become Hibernia, I was a young lieutenant in the navy. I drove a small Renault car. I could fill the tank for less that $5. You could buy a four-bedroom house for $15,000 and you could have a sumptuous meal in a restaurant for less than $35, including tip. That was a long time ago and a lot of things have happened in the interim.
What I would like to do today, in the capacities that I mentioned and on third reading of this bill, is address myself to the package that has become Hibernia. I want to speak to the background and I want to give a more detailed description of what it is. I think there is a general combination of misunderstanding and, if not a lack of knowledge, a thirst for knowledge of exactly what this project is going to do.
I want to speak to some of the reservations regarding the project, in general for megaprojects and this one in particular, many of which were raised in the House. I want to go into some detail regarding the employment opportunities and the potential that this project has both in the short term and in the long term. Then I want to wrap up with a summary of the project's commitment to
Canada. I will parallel in many respects the comments that were made by the hon. minister, but I am delighted to report that my comments are not repetitive in the sense that they are the same as his, but if you talk about Hibernia, it does follow the same general pattern. Therefore, for the organizational sense of those listening, that will be the structure.
To begin with, Hibernia P15 was the sixtieth well drilled in the Newfoundland and Labrador offshore area. Between 1980 and 1984, in eight of nine delineation wells-a delineation well is when you drill out to see how far the resource extends-they encountered significant quantities of oil, to their entire satisfaction. Even at that time, the recoverable reserves were estimated to be between 525 million and 650 million barrels.
In May 1985, Mobil Oil Canada, on behalf of the Hibernia consortium, submitted economical and environmental impact studies to the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador. These studies in turn led to public hearings and to the release of a document entitled: The Report of the Hibernia Environmental Assessment Panel in January 1986. A downstream development plan, including a benefits plan, was submitted to the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board-and for future reference I will just call it the offshore petroleum board-in September 1985 and subject to the resolution of certain technical, employment and industrial benefit issues, that I will speak to later, was given the Offshore Petroleum Board approval in general in June 1986.
Two years later, in July 1988, the consortium-that is, the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, plus the oil consortia- signed the Hibernia statement of principles which established the general terms and conditions under which the development would take place. As an aside, I was in the Hotel Newfoundland on that particular day and I must confess it was a day of great jubilation and a day of great hope. While we have had to wait a little longer than was promised for that, I believe we would agree, it has been worth the wait.
Subsequent to the signing of the statement of principles, as the hon. minister mentioned, the platform topside facilities were redesigned from, I think, 22 smaller modules to five supermodules. This revised plan was submitted to the Offshore Petroleum Board in March 1990 and was approved in August of this year.
October 4, 1990

Since the signing of this statement of principles, all parties have been negotiating to finalize the legal agreements. The agreement announced on September 14, again in another atmosphere of great hope and jubilation in fact that this was more progress in what hopefully will soon be the final enabling legislation for this project, allowed the project to proceed. All the agreements, including those related to royalties, financing, industrial benefits and related matters have been finalized, and as the hon. minister said, placed in escrow pending passage of Bill C-44-that is what we are in the process of doing now-by the Parliament of Canada.
What happened on September 14? The three parties entered into an initial engineering development and project agreement using the offshore development fund from which they borrowed $95 million. This was made available to the consortium to cover its costs until parliamentary approval is obtained and the agreements are formally executed. This will happen when Bill C-44 goes through the Parliament of Canada and, hopefully, that is not long away. At that time any moneys advanced will be repaid and by this mechanism the way has been cleared to allow the project to proceed immediately.
The Hibernia development plan envisages a concrete platform, 83 development wells, a crude oil loading system, sub-sea facilities and three specially built shuttle tankers of 120,000 tonnes. The platform will be designed to produce a maximum of 150,000 barrels of oil per day and withstand harsh environmental forces, including the impact of icebergs. Storage facilities for 1.3 million barrels of oil will be provided within the platform base itself, representing storage for approximately two weeks of production. It is estimated that an average of 110,000 barrels of oil per day will be expected during the peak production period.
The pre-production capital expenditures are estimated to total approximately $5.2 billion and that will be spent between 1990 and 1996. A further $3.3 billion in capital expenditures will be incurred after production begins. After production begins, the operating phase expenditures are estimated to total around $10 billion
Government Orders
over the projected 18 to 20-year production life of the oil field.
Two major project contracts have been awarded, one for the engineering and construction of the gravity based structure, and the other for the project management and topside engineering. As I have said many times in the House, and I am very proud to say, the work on the construction and assembly site near Bull Arm and Great Mosquito Cove is expected to begin now.
The expenditures and resulting oil revenues will boost the economies in all parts of Canada. Although there is no question that Newfoundland will benefit from this perhaps more than any other province, Hibernia will provide business opportunity to shipyards, equipment suppliers, cement producers, and hundreds of other businesses throughout the country. Canadian goods and services will account for, as the minister said, 60 per cent to 65 per cent of the project expenditure during construction, and over 65 per cent during its operation. This is double what happened in previous megaproject examples. Most of the people employed during the construction will be Canadian residents, Newfoundlanders, and it is expected that most workers during the operations will be the same.
As part of the introduction, I think I can safely say, and I think there is general agreement, that the Newfoundland offshore opportunity that I am discussing here presents new challenges, not just in Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces, but to the whole Canadian petroleum industry. Hibernia will meet these challenges and will put Canada, Newfoundland, and Labrador on the leading edge of offshore technology.
At this point in time, I want to bring up the subject of the controversy that this megaproject has conjured up. I am not surprised. I think anyone who has been involved in a megaproject before should not be surprised. You are dealing with a lot of money. You are dealing with technological advances. You are dealing with state of the art technology, and you are dealing with human factors. You are dealing with bruised egos. You are dealing with the not-invented-here syndrome. You are dealing with people who are competing for contracts, companies that

October 4, 1990
Government Orders
are competing for opportunities, and people who are competing for jobs. The stakes are high. It is a big poker game, and in big poker games, in big games of chance, the emotions are high, the stress is high. The arguments are big and long and go into the night. This is what we have here, because we are dealing with something that will happen 25 years from now.
Look at what happened last year in the world. People were saying that Germany would never unify. That was a year ago and it happened yesterday. The uncertainty in dealing with the world today and one year from now is complex and there are so many surprises. Good heavens, 25 years from now is very uncertain. We are dealing with risk and uncertainty. When dealing with risk and uncertainty-and I have been trained in that area-one has to make certain assumptions and you have to take certain chances. This is what is happening in the Hibernia project.
I want to talk about two aspects of this. The first is the technological advances. The hon. minister said not too long ago that politicians were sometimes accused of overstating the case. I will quote a gentleman who is fairly well known, C. K. Chesterton. He who said that there are times and circumstances when it is necessary to exaggerate in order to reveal the truth.
The enduring truth today in the growth of technology is undeniable. I just want to give some indication of this and I appreciate that there are a lot of people here who are trained in this business, but equally there are a lot of people who are trained in the arts and humanities side. I think it would be perhaps instructive to give some indication of what we are dealing with, the sheer range of technology in the world today.
We are probing phenomena that are as small as 10-15 centimetre. That is a hundred thousandth of a billionth of a centimetre. We can deal with things so small that there are systems in the world today that will allow one to etch a million angels on the head of a common pin. That is mind-boggling. I cannot really conceive that, but it can happen. That is on the small side.
On the large side we are dealing with a universe the edge of which, we are told, is 10 with 23 zeros, 1023 miles away. If I am right, that is 10,000 billion, billion miles away. So, we have this minute capability in a universe that is just endless.
It is similar with time. We are studying phenomena so short-lived that today it occurs in 10-23 of a second. By contrast, our astronomers and our astrologers tell us that the universe is 20 billion years old.
The sheer scale of explorable nature has burst beyond yesterday's wildest assumptions and imaginations. No where is this better illustrated than the world of the computer, and the computer is a very large part of this system that we are dealing with.
It was recently noted that the Industrial Revolution increased productivity by a factor of 100, while the microchip has raised data base technology by a factor of one million. Today a single microchip has the capacity of one million transistors and, it is estimated that in about 10 years time, it will have the capacity of one billion transistors. Perhaps I could be more illustrative on this point.
In 1960 the computing capacity that would run the battle control system of a modern warship would fill the area the average living room. That was in 1960. By 1980, 20 years later, it could probably fit on the top of two desks. Today, it can fit in one of those very razor-thin briefcases. The cost in 1960 was around $5 million. In 1980, it was around $100,000, and today, about $1,000 or less.
It was estimated that if the automobile industry had done what the computer industry had done in the past 30 years, a Rolls-Royce would cost $2.50 and would get two million miles to the gallon. That is the kind of strides that have been made.
Again, we talk about $5.2 billion and $3.3 billion. We throw them around. What is the difference between $5.2 billion and $5.1, or $5.3? As politicians, program managers, and business administrators, we use these terms. I can imagine $1 million, I can see it over there in the corner, in $1 bills or $100 bills. But $1 billion is very difficult for me to conceive, so I sat down last night and I tried to work it out in a metaphysical sense so I could appreciate what $1 billion would mean. This is what it means to me in two senses, in time and in space.
If I took $100 bills when I was 40 years of age and started counting them, one every second, I would be 70 years of age before I counted $1 billion. In terms of space, if you took $100 bills and put them end to end and went around the equator, do you know how many times you could go around, Mr. Speaker? Two hundred and seventy-fives times, with $100 bills end to end. That is what we are dealing with. And we are dealing with 5.2 of those in the design and construction phase, and 3.3 of
October 4, 1990

them in the production phase. Mind-boggling, Mr. Speaker, absolutely mind-boggling.
There is another pragmatic thought which is relevant to the subject because it gives some indication of the kind of technology we are dealing with today in this project and why there are so many uncertainties, and why there are criticisms and rightly so.
Ninety per cent of the body of knowledge that exists in the world today has been created since I left high school. It will double again before I become eligible for the old age pension. That gives some indication of how rapidly the world of knowledge is expanding. Something is designed today and by the time it is produced, it is out of date. If it is not totally outdated, it is in the process of becoming so. Whether it is one year or ten years, as in the case of ships that I am familiar with, it is designed for something and, by the time it is built, it is not the same state of the art.
There is something more disturbing perhaps, and I am sorry to have to report this, but I hear it from university professors and presidents of universities and I feel I stand on good ground when I make this statement.
There is no doubt that the technological leadership in any country has become a strategic factor in determining the economic performance of a country, a region or a province. In this regard, I regret to say that Canada lags behind its industrial competitors. Atlantic Canada, in particular, lags behind other provinces in its per capita basis in production and retention of human resources. In Canada, on a per capita basis, we employ one-half the number of engineers and scientists that our competitors employ. Let me talk about one aspect of which I am very familiar.
Although we are the world's largest fish exporter, it was suggested at a recent conference that Canada's fisheries are now where Europe's were 15 years ago. Think about what our fishing industry could be doing without this technological lag. Think about the kinds of fisheries policies we could have without this impediment. Think about what addressing this problem alone could do for Newfoundland and all its communities, none of which are unaffected by the fisheries.
Government Orders
We are dealing with technology, sophistication, and cost that it is almost impossible for any one but the totally brilliant to be able to grasp, integrate, conceptualize, work out assumptions to cope with the uncertainties, do the risk analysis and to manage.
I would like to address some of the difficulties that my colleagues have had with this project. Members from the NDP expressed concerns about the amount of money invested and the risk that we are taking as a government. They have also expressed some concerns about the environment. In fact, I was very upset to hear that they were not really for this project. I hope when they campaign in Newfoundland, whenever the next election is going to be, they will remember that they did not support this project. I hope it has developed, at that point in time, where a lot of these uncertainties have disappeared and the early benefits of this project will be evident, not just for Newfoundland or eastern or Atlantic Canada, but indeed for the whole of Canada.
I had to satisfy myself before I spoke in support of this bill that there had been studies done, assumptions made, and money spent on the environmental aspects of this. I, too, have concerns about the fishing industry. One cannot go into this with blindfolds on. I satisfied myself that, yes, there is always risk, but I believe the risk has been minimized. I would like to tell you about what I know about this particular aspect. It is an uncertainty and it it something that has been discussed at length in the House. I am speaking now about the environmental aspect.
The governments of Canada and Newfoundland, the main partners in this, decided that an environmental impact on the Hibernia project should be reviewed by a joint federal-provincial environment assessment panel. Mobil Oil, the head honcho in this, representing the Hibernia consortium, conducted environmental studies and they produced an environmental impact statement. These documents were reviewed publicly by the joint federal-provincial panel at hearings held throughout Newfoundland. In December, 1985, almost five years ago, the panel concluded that the Hibernia project should proceed. That was not the end of it, it went on from there. The Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office, called FERO for short, recently reviewed the 1986 panel report and, they concluded that the report was prepared in accordance with the environmental assessment and review process, EARP for short, and they were happy with it. The Canada-Newfoundland

October 4, 1990
Government Orders
Offshore Petroleum Board, I will refer to it as the offshore petroleum board for short, reviewed the Hibernia development plan, which was submitted in December of 1985, and it approved the development plan in June of 1986.
Mobil Oil then submitted the development plan update in March, 1990. The offshore petroleum board decided that the update constituted a revised development plan requiring board approval. It then carried out a detailed environmental review of the update and submitted, to federal and provincial ministers, this update. This was then reviewed under the EARP guidelines by the Canadian oil and gas lands administration as the lead initiating agency.
The whole point of this is that this review was co-ordinated with other departments, it got public input, and there was prepared an initial screening decision, as required by the EARP guidelines. The Canadian oil and gas lands administration concluded, and here is the kicker, that there are no significant environmental effects identified at this stage of the project review. It did not say that there were none, it said that there were "no significant", and that was enough to let the project proceed.
Now there have been other concerns expressed in this House with, perhaps, the same magnitude as those concerns expressed about the environmental impact of this particular project. These had to do with why we have to settle for 25 per cent of this and 40 per cent of that and the totality, even of 65 per cent Canadian input in the whole project.
I was somewhat disappointed that this deficiency or apparent deficiency, or concern, was not really addressed and I think it was not addressed because time did not permit. We were speaking on motions, amendments to motions, and amendments to amendments to motions, and I think sometimes the impact of the concern gets lost in the procedure. I am not great on procedure myself, Mr. Speaker. Procedure is all good stuff and I know that you are very learned in this area. I am interested in the substance and I have hon. members, such as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, who instruct me
on procedure. I regret the hon. member is not here today so if I mess up in procedure, you will have to forgive me.
I would like this bill to leave the House of Commons after third reading with, if not the sort of political support of those members who are somewhat recalcitrant about this project, at least with their support for the spirit of the project. They may vote against it at third reading but I would like to believe that they have the spirit. This is the reason I am addressing their concerns. I could gloss over them, I could leave them out, I could speak only about the good things about this project, but I am a realist, as I said yesterday, and I want to speak to this. I want it on the record and I want them to hear the concerns and why we get 65 per cent and not 100 per cent Canadian content.
I want to talk about two things; materials, that is the raw materials, the steel and the concrete bars, and the equipment, that is the generators, the man-made equipment. These are two separate items. Let me talk about the materials first.
The price of the materials required for this project will total around $300 million. That is a lot of money. These materials include such things as steel plate, pipe and piping, casing, cement, wire, cable, valves and instrumentation. These are the raw materials for this project. More than 30 per cent, by value, of the steel plate and tubulars required for the structure is available from mills throughout Canada, that is the availability factor.
In addition, Canadian suppliers are capable of producing smaller diameter well casing which accounts for about 50 per cent of the smaller casing requirements. Seventy-five per cent of valve requirements can be supplied by Canadian sources. However, there are some limitations. Heavy duty ball valves may not be available in Canada and the ballast water and other sea water piping, fittings and valves, used on the platform will likely be made of titanium or austenitic stainless steel which is currently, to my knowledge, not available in Canada.
I think the important thing here is that the Canadian supply capability in instrumentation-these are the valves, dials, readouts and printouts that we get-varies
October 4, 1990

widely, according to the item. The average capability is estimated at between 65 per cent and 75 per cent.
We range on availability in Canada right now between 30 per cent and 75 per cent of the materials needed for this project.
I think, Mr. Speaker, you have heard a couple of members say in this House that the project will require about 100,000 tonnes of cement which will be supplied by plants in Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, as well as Newfoundland, and approximately 50,000 tonnes of reinforcing bar and prestressed cable for the precast concrete that will be needed. That can be supplied by Canadian companies all across the country.
That is the limitation in materials. Again, as I said yesterday, I am familiar with this because I have been involved in shipbuilding and construction of major projects. You cannot get all of the materials from one country, no matter which country you build it in. You have to go offshore to buy areas of expertise that other countries have become experts in. I see nothing wrong with that. This is part of the international order.
I would like to talk about equipment now, Mr. Speaker. These are ready built equipment, motors, generators and that sort of thing. Again, in dealing with the Hibernia project, we are looking at another $300 million. I will give you some examples. Some of the equipment will be pressure vessels, compressors, pumps, motors, electrical units, drilling, well equipment and that sort of category.
While some of this highly specialized equipment will have to be imported, the Canadian industry throughout the country has demonstrated the capability to produce a wide range of the equipment required by Hibernia. This has been done because we have been involved, albeit not in the same magnitude that we anticipate in the future, in offshore development. I told you that when it started, life was simpler and 25 years does a lot to a number of things, but it has allowed us to produce and to develop in this area. Had we started today, I would suggest that we would be back to where the Norwegians and the Brits were, with 30 per cent and maybe even 25 per cent.
We have companies in western Canada, for example, who can supply drilling equipment, such as rotary tables, oil and gas processing equipment, pressure vessels, separators, storage tanks, heat exchangers and trans-
Government Orders
formers, as well as some types of control systems. Why? Because they have been involved in the oil and gas system since the Leduc days in the 1940s. So it is only reasonable that they can do that. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I have a friend living in western Canada who is in the business of supplying this equipment and I have known him for 25-30 years. He was at it from the time I first knew him.
Companies in central Canada can be suppliers for such items as valves, pumps, compressors, switch gear and power generation units at which they are very good because of their industrial capacity. These are standard industrial items.
Companies in Atlantic Canada are potential suppliers of pumps, smaller valves, tanks and pressure vessels, because as you are aware, Mr. Speaker, we do have some shipyards in the Atlantic provinces. In fact, we are very good at that business. So these would be fallouts from that particular aspect of the industry.
Again, to summarize, it is estimated that between 40 per cent to 60 per cent of the components of the drilling package in the equipment area could be manufactured in Canada, indeed across Canada; from western Canada all across this great country.
Canadian capability in sub-sea equipment is limited, particularly to assembly of units, because most of the major components have been developed in the United States and in the U.K.. They have been in the offshore oil drilling business a lot longer than we have been. It is logical and understandable.
Generally speaking, current domestic capability in sub-sea equipment is estimated at between 30 per cent to 40 per cent. I think the point here is that as we jump into the pool and get ourselves concerned about draining the pool or the alligators, we will develop this. There will be mistakes made along the way. There will be people who will be hurt. There will be contracts that will overrun in cost and time. I can almost guarantee that. But that is the nature of megaprojects.
I do not like to dwell on my personal experience but I will have to report to you, Mr. Speaker, that 10 years ago I was the project director, not the program manager, but the project director of the Canadian Frigate Program. Members would know that we are talking of the same magnitude as the $5.2 billion for Hibernia.

October 4, 1990
Government Orders
I experienced in that a lot of uncertainty, a lot of difficulties in the very concept of a patrol frigate. There were those who said we do not need them. There were those who said we need bigger and fewer, and those who said we need more and less capable. The minister has to make a judgment. I have to make a judgment. My colleagues, everybody in the House here, civil servants who support the minister, people like myself and all those involved with this have to make a judgment. This is judgmental.
There is no computer that says you are doing it right, or you are doing it wrong. There is no computer that will guarantee that the minister, if he is still here as the minister two or three years from now, will have to get up in the House and answer some embarrassing questions. I can almost guarantee that will happen and I might be the person asking them, but that is part of the system.
I want to guarantee anybody who is here and listening to me that that always happens with a project of this kind. The way not to make it happen is not to do the project and then you will not make any mistakes. I do not operate that way. I am prepared to take a risk. God knows, I have made many mistakes in my life, I will probably make some more, and I can guarantee that there will be mistakes on this project, but let us get on with it and let us get it moving.
Mr. Speaker, I know it is getting close to one o'clock, but I want to get into an area now that is of vital concern to every member in this House. We know the employment situation in Canada. I am not making political hay, but the unemployment figures are up a little bit. They are terrible in Newfoundland and I am not saying this for political reasons. I am saying this as a lead in to the employment opportunities and the training opportunities that are under way. People call me on the telephone. Last night, when I got back from a reception after the House closed down, I got a call from one of my constituents. He said, "Can you tell me what is going on with Hibernia. How do you get a job? When are we going to start training for this?"
We do have foresight in Newfoundland. We have a thing called the Cabot Institute, a great institution that has graduated 20,000 people since the mid-sixties. In
fact, just two hours ago I spoke with the president, Dr. Linda Inkpen and she indicated to me some of the things that are going on. We have been training people for a year and some to have the skills in Newfoundland and indeed in eastern Canada that are specifically related to the Hibernia project and in some of the spin-off areas like hotel management, hospitality management and just general business management of a kind that could look after some of the spin-off areas that would emanate from Hibernia.
Again, Mr. Speaker, one other point before I get into the detail of this. I have to make this point passionately. I am a believer of hands-on information. Something means more to me if I go to see it, touch it and get a feeling for it than if somebody tells me about it or I read it in a book. I live in Newfoundland. As I stand in this House this morning, there are 42,000 people that do not have jobs. There are 42,000 people that get up in the morning and have no place to go, except perhaps the post office to pick up their mail and chat with their colleagues. Regrettably some of the post offices are closing down, so they do not even have that to do these days.
Mr. Speaker, you and I have a job, and I expect we have always had a job. We have not experienced that. I would suggest that-you say, maybe not. If you have, then to experience the feeling of waking up in the morning and not having a job, I am told, is a terrible feeling and there are 42,000 people like that in Newfoundland. They speak to me. A lot of them are in my riding.
This project, to me, the centrefold of this project-if it were a Playboy magazine or a magazine of any kind, an automobile magazine-the centrefold is really the number of jobs and the hope that stems from these jobs.
Mr. Speaker, you would probably want to call it one o'clock and I will continue after Question Period.

Mr. Speaker, this week is National Family Week and therefore a wonderful opportunity for me to pay special tribute to a remarkable Quebec family headed by Ms. Louise Brissette.
This 44 year old single woman, a physiotherapist and osteopath, has adopted 14 handicapped children. Only five are able to eat unassisted. Three can walk, but the others are in wheelchairs. The children have major handicaps, but this courageous woman says that, to her, a handicapped child is like a poorly-wrapped gift, a human being encased in an imperfect shell, but nevertheless part of the marvelous world God has created, part of Creation.
A tireless worker and an example to us all, Ms. Brissette plans to open a centre this fall in Sillery to provide temporary accommodation for handicapped children and their parents.
Mr. Speaker, we wish Ms. Louise Brissette and her fourteen children, her "real" family as she points out, all the happiness and success they deserve.

Mr. Speaker, today is the first sitting day of the new Parliament of the newly united Germany. The Parliament is sitting at the Reichstag in Berlin 45 years after the creation of and only 11 months after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
It was only fitting that on Monday following the ratification by the four allied powers preparations for the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe to be held in November were begun by the foreign ministers of the 35 participating states.
Canada looks forward to playing a significant role in the new Europe and, as assured to us by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, we will strive to achieve a commitment by the heads of state in obtaining new security arrangements for all of Europe and North America.
In closing, the House joins Canadians of German descent in congratulating Germans of former East and West Germany for this remarkable achievement. We share in their joy and hope that this unity will lead to greater prosperity and a better life for all Germans and for all peoples of Europe.

Mr. Speaker, Roman Emperor Caligula tried to appoint his horse as consul of ancient Rome. This was probably legal because he was the dictator at the time.
This government has packed the Canadian Senate with eight extra Tory horses, now called honourable senators, but is it legal? Does the fact that this extraordinary power has never been used in 126 years make it inoperative? A former Supreme Court judge says that may well be true.
By appointing extra senators from New Brunswick-more than they have members of Parliament-is that a constitutional amendment done unilaterally and therefore would be unconstitutional? The legal experts differ. Even the Minister of Justice is confused about this issue.
We in the NDP believe it is irresponsible for government to proceed with the GST without a court reference on its legality. Why take the chance that later acts of Parliament could be illegal or unconstitutional. This will bring legal and economic instability.
Who does the Prime Minister think-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the August 20 General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade update seminar in Abbotsford, British Columbia, attended by over 700 farm producers, I have received 180-odd follow up letters seeking assurances that supply

October 4, 1990
management not be bargained away. I share this concern.
The Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Agriculture have continually pledged their commitment to fight for the integrity of supply management in Canada by seeking clarification and strengthening of article XI of the GAIT. I encourage the ministers and our negotiators at the GATT to do their utmost to ensure this position stays firm.
Further, we need to preserve the integrity of supply management by exempting supply managed commodities from the application of a damaging aggregate measure of support and by maintaining existing internal support and border measures which are the underpinnings of supply management.
I believe this stand is needed and appropriate.

Mr. Speaker, this past Sunday the world's first ever monument to human rights was unveiled here in the nation's capital. To be in attendance at the unveiling ceremony, the celebration dinner, and the human rights committee, where the Dalai Lama graced the members with his presence, was indeed a pleasure and a privilege.
Three years ago I was part of the negotiating process that secured the Elgin Street site. The hard work of George Wilkes and his committee for a monument to human rights, the chosen design of artist Melvin Char-ney, and the approval of regional government should each be recognized and commended by this House.
Nobel Peace Prize winner, the Dalai Lama of Tibet, is an outstanding example of dedication to non-violence, conciliation, and maintenance of human rights. Canada should take the initiative in its bilateral relations with China to support the intent of the Dalai Lama's five-point plan for greater Tibetan autonomy and help
facilitate a more constructive dialogue between China and the Tibetan people.

Mr. Speaker, the cause for national unity in Canada prevails more strongly than ever.
In recent months feelings of alienation have intensified in many quarters, not only in Quebec but among native Indians and between regions of the country as well. The search for Canada's vision goes on in Quebec, in New Brunswick, and all across the nation.
This is a process that should be encouraged. It will not be harmful. In fact it will be helpful that citizens throughout Canada stop to reflect seriously about the kind of country we really want and, more important, about how we can attain our vision.
As these examinations mature I am confident that this federal government will lead the consensus toward the obvious reality of a national vision which will express our country's collective and united will as a whole.
I believe that history will reveal we are even now at work in Canada to build a special nation, one that will be a model for the world.
To reach that destiny we must each take a stand. I stand firmly for one united country. In my opinion there is no tolerable alternative for Canada's future.

Mr. Speaker, something is wrong when readers and writers across this country have to rely on the unelected Senate to block the GST which will do irrepairable damage to their industry.
Quebec's advisory council on books and literature, among others, has stated that sales of French books will decline by 25 per cent, which will have a disastrous impact on Quebec's culture. Similar effects will be felt by the scientific community throughout Canada, Mr. Speaker.
October 4, 1990

This dire warning of the council echoes those of Quebec Cultural Affairs Minister Lucienne Robillard, the PQ opposition, the Quebec writers' union, and the coalition against taxes on books.
When will the government finally withdraw this harmful bill?

Mr. Speaker, there is some pressure to reopen the memorandum of understanding between U.S. and Canada regarding the forestry industry.
However, there are strong economic national reasons for maintaining the memorandum of understanding for the long-term good of Canada's forestry industry.

Before we called it one o'clock earlier this afternoon, I had risen to speak as the associate energy critic and as the member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception where a large part of the construction of Hibernia will take place, to address elements of the project that had concerned a lot of people. I went through some background. I covered some of the details that perhaps were not well known to the House and, indeed, to the public. Then, I specifically covered two areas concerning members of the House, perhaps with the indication and certainly the aim of putting their minds at rest and to make them feel more supportive of this project. After all, it is going to be going on for 25 years.
Just before one o'clock, I looked at the materials and the equipment for this project that will total some $600 million. I gave what I believe to be the reasons why we physically cannot make this a 100 per cent project, purely in the area of materials and equipment.
I will now talk about what certainly in the interim period-the construction and production phase- will be the most important aspect to a lot of Newfoundlanders, to a lot of Atlantic Canadians, and indeed to all Canadians, but I may add the least understood aspect of this
particular megaproject. I am referring to of course the employment opportunities.
I read in The Globe and Mail this morning, for example, an article with this headline: "Thousands scramble for few Hibernia jobs". The gist of the article is that there are thousands of people lining up and before the end of this year, it states that there will be only anywhere from 40 to 60 jobs.
I welcome the opportunity to speak on this because I have been following this project for a long time. I have spoken to members on the other side of the House, to the hon. ministers involved in this, to the hon. members, my own colleagues here, members of industry, bureaucrats, and those involved in the actual doing of this project. I hope, I say in all modesty, what I have to say will be instructive and informative.
It is well known that Hibernia will create thousands of employment opportunities across Canada. These opportunities will be offered generally, not by Mobil Oil, but by the major contractors or the service companies working on the project. I think that is a very important point. Most of the jobs during the development phase will fall into one of five industrial categories: construction, shipbuilding, manufacturing, engineering, and offshore contracting. There will be a wide range of skills and skill levels that will be required over the six-year project development schedule and during the approximate 20 years of production. I think it would be worthwhile perhaps to get into that in more detail, but, on a general note, employment on the project is measured in terms of person-years.
There sometimes is confusion as to what a person-year is. Very simply, one-year's employment for one person equals one person-year. Sometimes a million of manhours is the term used, but I will deal with person-years, exclusively, so that we do not switch from one measure to the other.
During the development phase, the project will create an estimated 21,500 person-years of employment with 14,500 of those expected to be in Canada. According to the project schedule, the demand will begin to grow late this year. I have to use a range and am told that it will be between 40 and 100, depending on how rapidly the project gets under way and, indeed, what the weather is going to be like in November and December. But the employment is expected to peak in about 1993-1994, with work on several activities occurring at the same time in different locations.

The first six-year phase, the development phase, from now to 1995-1996, can be broken down into seven main activities. First is the gravity base structure, that is, the big concrete platform that is going to be launched, towed out to sea, and sunk in about 250 feet of water, 80 metres of water. This will employ 4,545 person-years. For the topsides that are built onto the gravity base structure it will be 6,305.
There is the articulated loading platform. From this gravity base structure and the modules that I just described will be an undersea component, a manifold, and 1.3 million tonnes will be stored in the gravity base structure itself. The large tankers, of which there will be three at 120,000 tonnes, a fair-sized ship, will load from what is called the articulated loading platforms that are going to be spaced some distance from the gravity base structure itself. Of course, associated with that will be a pipeline, and there will be 290 man-hours.
For the sub-sea manifolds, the mechanism under the sea that is involved in the flow of the light crude oil that will go to the articulated loading platform, there will be 1,110. Then, for the drilling itself, there will be 1,650 and for the vessel construction to which I made reference, the three 120,000 tonne shuttle tankers, 450 man-years. Quite frankly, I think that is conservative but I will use the figures that I was given two days ago. For the startup there will be 150. That comprises the 14,500.
I know there are people listening to this who would like to know with what kind of trades are we dealing. With the indulgence of the Chair, I would like to give you some indication of the trades that are involved. They range from management administration to carpenters. I will just read out some of them: management adminis-
