tricians, welders, pipe fitters and heavy equipment operators. I know a lot of heavy equipment operators in the area who will be looking forward to getting some work in this area.

While it is not in my riding, I know the people from Argentia. Mr. Speaker, I want to speak very briefly to the training and the experience required. From the perspective of training and experience, the jobs created by Hibernia will vary widely from occupation to occupation. I want to use these examples from one end of the spectrum to the other. Senior managers and engineers will ordinarily require engineering degrees and several years of direct experience in the design and construction of offshore facilities. Some of the key fabrication and construction occupations will require journeymen status or equivalent and, in addition, may require some upgrading skills to meet special certification standards.
For the other occupations, the standard requirement of the particular industry, whether it is construction or steel fabrication, I expect will be sufficient. That is what is envisaged by the project management team right now.
During the development phase of the project, the major activities that I made reference to, for example, the gravity base structure, will rely largely on the mechanical and civil trades available in the construction industry. The skill levels and mechanical outfitting are required to be higher in some cases but the standard requirement is sufficient in others.
Module fabrication will require mainly the steel fabrication trades, plate and pipefitters, welders, riggers and electricians. Again the skill levels required are high, particularly for fitters and welders.
Then we come to the topside assembly which will require mainly mechanical trades involved in marine fabrication. It is likely that many of those skills, particularly the fitters, welders and electricians will require some upgrading in order to qualify for the jobs with the state of the art techniques required.
In the closing moments of my presentation, I want to just give you some indication of what preparations have taken place in Newfoundland. I am sure that other preparations have taken place across Canada, and I am aware of some of them, but I am directly involved in the preparations taking place in Newfoundland. I just want to make reference to one institution that is well known. I made reference to it this morning, the Cabot Institute.

In 1989 the faculty and administrative staff of the Cabot Institute authorized a strategic plan for the year 2000, which is the time frame for this particular project. The impact of the offshore oil development was a major consideration which influenced the over-all contents of the document. This was worked on for over four years. The people involved worked with management and with the knowledge of the skills required, they travelled to North American and European offshore construction and production sites. Some of the faculty members received on-site training themselves in such diverse disciplines as well logging, dimensional control, pipefitting, structural welding, project management, computer aided design and drafting, computer aided manufacturing and quality assurance and quality control.
As part of this, the computer facilities at Cabot itself have been substantially upgraded and are currently considered to be the best, certainly in our provincial college system, and could rate with any of those in eastern Canada. I may be challenged on that, but I know they are certainly of a very high quality.
There are some other specific things that have been done, again in the Cabot Institute, to make ready the system of education and training in Newfoundland for this project. I mentioned the strategic plan and I will not expand on that any more.
There is a second computer assisted drafting and design lab that recently was installed to serve all the engineering technologies. Riely's Datashare of Calgary-and here we have some involvement from western Canada-has agreed to make available to Cabot Institute a database with a commercial value of $750,000 containing data from over 20 wells in the Hibernia and related geological structures. This, with the relatively scant knowledge I have of the oil drilling operation, is an invaluable resource that will be used by students in the petroleum engineering technology. Another thing, again at the Cabot Institute, a state of the art geographical information system has been purchased and forms the basis of a revised survey and engineering technology program. All other engineering technologies will be made aware of the versatility of the computer software that is involved in this program.

We have another item. This institute has enthusiastically endorsed the introduction of the co-operative education program. In fact, in September it introduced its first co-operative education program, a three-year, eight-term program in computer studies. I do not have to tell you the importance of computers in the operation of this business and in the instrumentation involved. They have a steering committee that will target further current offerings for delivery through co-operative education in 1991 and every year to follow. They have an advisory committee set up specifically to oversee skills related to the Hibernia project. They have other areas, as well.
I spoke with the president of the institute just this morning and I was quite impressed by many of the concerns it has. It is concerned that the appropriate labour relations, education, and training will continue to be offered as part of most, if not all, their 60 programs that they have, with a specific eye on what is required for Hibernia.
Such information will be timely, relevant, and appropriately imparted to give their students a clearer understanding of the labour climate within which they will work and to which they will contribute. It will be to no student's benefit to be denied relevant facts on basic labour relations theory and practice as it concerns management and workers. A labour relations management, of course, would do well to address more fully these issues as we get downstream and more people are employed in these activities.
With respect to the Cabot Institute, during the next few years many of the businesses and companies that will most probably be involved in the Hibernia project will be affected by the graduates of this institute. They have not forgotten their traditional programs and they must continue to educate and train Newfoundlanders, Labradorians, and indeed mainlanders who attend the institute for non-oil related jobs. These are the businesses that will be a spinoff from the project itself. It has been said that perhaps the largest workforce adjustment will occur as indirect effects of Hibernia. Homes must continue to be designed and built and carpenters, electricians and plumbers will continue to work in non-oil related occu-

pations. Business establishments will continue to require quality secretarial and business graduates, and all the education and training facilities must not just reflect Hibernia but the spillovers that will pertain to Hibernia.
Before I wrap up, I would like to summarize one of the main concerns that is pertained in this House from November 7 of last year, which is almost a year ago when we first started to discuss this project. Some will say it is a relatively short time, but it has been the style of the House. It went through first and second reading and committee stage. While some may disagree with the length of time it took, we are now at this stage and third reading.
The one thread that went through this whole thing was the project's commitment to Canada. I think there were well founded suspicions. I never impute the motives of those people who are concerned about how we spend the taxpayers' money. I would like to cover basically what the project's commitment is to Canada.
I take great comfort from the knowledge that I have of this project, but I would like to emphasize that this is a megaproject. There are risks and benefits involved. At this point in time, as we search out into the uncertainty, we on this side of the House believe and I am sure many of my colleagues believe that the benefits are greater than the risks. The Governments of Canada and Newfoundland and Labrador have entered into an agreement with Mobil Oil and the joint venture participants on the development of Hibernia.
A lot of this will be summary, but as a result of the fiscal agreement the Government of Canada will contribute 25 per cent of the pre-production capital costs, up to a value of $1 billion. It will guarantee loans for 40 per cent of the pre-production capital costs, up to a maximum guarantee of $1.7 billion. The Government of Newfoundland and Labrador will remove the retail sales tax on project capital costs, reduce the retail sales tax on operating costs to 4 per cent, accept a price sensitive royalty regime, and provide $10 million to the project for specific engineering activities in the province. In return, the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador will earn net revenues from the project of between $2.6 billion and $5.1 billion, based on 1987 oil prices. I have not yet got the projections for the present oil prices. I
can only assume that they will be greater. These are conservative estimates.
Both governments will also earn a substantial share of the profits if the oil prices surge again, which they are now doing, but who knows where they are going to be 20 years from now, and if the reserves prove larger than expected.
I would have to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that I believe like the song says: "This is going to be the start of something big." We know there are two more oil fields. Twenty miles south of Hibernia is the Terra Nova oil field, and not far from the Terra Nova oil field is the Ben Nevis oil field. Who knows, we believe there are more out there.
These revenue figures basically refer to the tax principles and the royalties involved. They do not include the economic benefits that accrue from the creation of jobs or industrial opportunities for individual firms.
As a result of the negotiations that were recently concluded, the commitments to Canada and Newfoundland benefits were reinforced, and certain aspects were incorporated as formal undertakings. These undertakings are summarized.
Regarding the employment and the procurement benefits, in a sense fair opportunity is given where fair opportunity can be given. Indeed, the best efforts are being made to achieve the Canadian and Newfoundland target content on a competitive basis of 45 per cent to 50 per cent. This includes the estimated 40 per cent to 50 per cent of module fabrication and up to 90 per cent and maybe 100 per cent of fabrication of decks and preassemblies in the outfitting of the concrete base.
They are to have their performance with respect to these targets monitored by the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board, which will examine reasons for possible shortfalls and measures to overcome them.
I will say now I am aware that the Newfoundland government is setting up a combination of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in Newfoundland provincially. I do not know the structure or the details. I believe that there is work under way to set up a special monitoring team to make sure that this project does what it says it was going to do and what it really should be doing.

Then we have the main support frame, assembly and outfitting. Of course that will take place in Newfoundland.
The engineering itself is again to make the best efforts to achieve a target of 80 per cent to 90 per cent in Canada for project management. Engineering design is for the gravity base structure, topsides and the articulated loading platform that I described earlier along with the subsea pipelines.
Fifty per cent of the gravity base structure design engineering and 100 per cent of the design engineering for the accommodation facilities-very important-flare boom, helideck and subsea export lines are in Newfoundland.
They are to package the engineering contracts, to promote participation of Canadian and Newfoundland businesses, to encourage the formation of national engineering consortia to qualify for the project, and to award the project services and topside engineering contract to a consortium with a majority Canadian equity participation and commensurate direction. That is in the process of happening now. In fact some of it has happened. Finally, they are to include the assessment of benefits as a key factor in the awarding of engineering contracts.
It has been my great privilege to stand in this House of Commons and to talk about this project. It is one that is dear to my heart. I know my colleagues support it. Many colleagues on both sides of the House see this as a vision that has come to fruition, a vision that is about to become a reality.
Again, I mentioned I was involved in two projects from the very beginning: the concept and the paper that now will be a Canadian patrol frigate program. It was written in 1977.1 first saw the frigate as a whole frigate 12 years later. I cannot convey to you, Mr. Speaker, the feeling of translating the vision and words on paper to something that is a reality.
I sense that perhaps it would be inadequate just to summarize and sort of say that I am finished.
I would like to quote King Solomon who I believe was recorded to have said: "Without vision the people perish." This was a vision, but I will say also that without jobs the people starve. Somewhere in between the vision and the jobs, there has been an awful lot of hard word that has gone on-and the hon. minister mentioned it
Government Orders
this morning-by politicians, by businessmen, by bureaucrats, by civil servants, by the average person in the field, by everybody involved.
I have not found any one person who has been touched by this project, who has been anything but positive. There are negative people, there are pessimists around and for reason. With the uncertainty involved, there are bound to be some people who will say it is not going to work, you are going to lose money, you are going to lose equalization payments or you will not get all those jobs. That is fair enough and I defend their right to feel that way, but I would say that as this project proceeds those who will be optimistic will far and increasingly outnumber those who are pessimistic about the success of this project and about the kind of benefits that we will derive from it.
There is a spirit in Hibernia. I call it the Hibernia spirit. People ask me: "Why is it called Hibernia". I say: "I don't know. I like the name Hibernia. I am sure there are all kinds of reasons for it". The spirit is there and the other thing that I sense is-I wish I could find a more musical, a more sophisticated, a more esoteric term to call it but I cannot-a psychological kick, and I like that psychological kick. I sense it in the province. I sense it on open line shows. I sense it in the newspaper, and I sense it in my colleagues when we talk about things.
One must not underestimate the power of confidence, both in the business world and among the general public. The tangible benefits of Hibernia itself may still be years away and sustained prosperity may yet still be a dream. I will acknowledge that, but the project will do its job if Canada in general and Newfoundland in particular can milk the mood of optimism and push the economic spectators and pessimists back into the playing field as we forge ahead with this omnipotent, wonderful, welcome, fantastic, project.

In setting out so to do I should like to note again for the record a brief remark delivered by the hon. minister close to the beginning of his speech this morning in which he, referring to all members that have participated in the debate over the Hibernia bill, said that they had "debated this bill but have always supported Hibernia".

Mr. Speaker, it is the bill that has received that opposition. We have no objection in principle to the Hibernia project. I wish that to be utterly clear.
Further, if a group of private sector proponents were to come to the Government of Canada and say: "Hey, Government of Canada, we've got all this money here. We want to build Hibernia," and if in so doing they were able to satisfy the EARP process, which by the way to this day has not been undertaken with regard to the Hibernia project, and if they were able to satisfy certain other social and economic criteria, fine, no problem. Let them at it.
But, Mr. Speaker, the minute a penny of public money becomes involved in a project, it is most legitimately the business of this House and it is the duty of the members of this House to closely consider the wisdom of the
Government Orders
regime under which it is proposed that public money be spent.
It is exactly the same thing as if I was to stumble into this House one day and say: "Hey, guys, gals, we got this plan out in Alberta. We are going to extract penicillin from cowhide. The only thing is we need a billion dollars. It is going to make all kinds of jobs. I mean, we are going to employ everybody from Coutts to Fort Chipewyan, but we do need the billion bucks."
I would expect that hon. members of this House would look at that, they would sort of scratch their chins and say: "Hm-m-m. Sounds a bit fuzzy but let's have a look."
That would be proper. It would be absolutely proper for the members of this House to adopt that attitude, which is precisely the attitude that the New Democratic Party caucus has adopted in this House. I am sorry if it has disappointed many of the hon. members here that we have declined to join in the hallelujah chorus in this instance, but it is a declination we shall maintain because the terms of the bill are inadequate. It is not a good deal for the people of Canada. In fact, it is a profoundly bad deal for the people of Canada.
I say this in the main because, right at the outset, the bill proposes to give $1,040 million to the proponents of the project. That is: give, Mr. Speaker. In the quaint language of the bill itself, it is called a "contribution". The same thing as "gift". That, we cannot support.
Time and time again I have raised the question, why not equity? If indeed the project is one that has merit- and we believe it is a project with merit - why then must we give the money away if government participation is required, and we are willing to accept the argument, given the risks involved and the huge capital nature of the project? Some public involvement is quite likely warranted. Why can we not invest it as, in fact, do the private sector proponents of the project?
Mobil Oil is not giving money to the Hibernia project. Petro-Canada is not giving money to the Hibernia project. They are investing money in the Hibernia project. It is only the people of Canada, through this bill and, I should note, the people of Newfoundland through the various concessions that have been wrested from their provincial government, that are giving away money to this project. It is not warranted because that public participation could easily be undertaken in the form of

October 4, 1990
Government Orders
equity, as has been the case in other energy megaprojects.
The Government of Ontario is a 25 per cent equity partner in the Suncor project, the very first of the large oil sands projects in northeastern Alberta. The government of Alberta, through its oil sands equity held by the trust fund is an equity participant in the Syncrude project. The Government of Canada is an equity participant to the tune of more than 31 per cent in the Lloydminster Bi-Provincial upgrader. All of these megaprojects have proceeded with public money. The difference is that in each instance that money has found its way into the project by way of equity earning a return for the people whose money it is; in this instance, the people of Canada.
I would note just in passing that in the 1980s the people of Alberta, from their 16 per cent share of the Syncrude project, reaped over $400 million net because of that equity participation. That is a tidy piece of change.
It is the sort of thing that could lighten the deficit load borne by our poor finance minister. But, no, Mr. Speaker, the bill before this House proposes simply to give that money away.
During the progress of this bill in this House and in committee, I could not help but be impressed by the wonderful congruence of interest apparently displayed by the Conservatives and the Liberals. There is a touching unanimity in this instance that has manifested itself in a number of ways and on a number of occasions from the merely obscurantist to the downright offensive.
In the former category, Mr. Speaker, I would refer you to the fact that on June 12, 1990, in committee, I directly questioned the Minister of Energy regarding the question of where the oil to be produced at Hibernia would go. I asked the minister, and I quote from the record of the committee:
What was the department's best estimate of the percentage of
Hibernia production that will be shipped to foreign market and
never seen in a Canadian refinery?
The minister answered:
Mr. Chairman, it is possible that some of the production over a given period of time entirely could go to a refinery other than Canadian, primarily refineries in the northeast United States. It will depend, quite frankly, on Canadian refineries bidding on some of that crude.
I asked the minister:
Have you a percentage?
The minister responded:
I do not think we do.
I asked the minister:
Have you a ballpark, a guess, a stab in the dark?
The minister responded:
It will only be that, Mr. Chairman, a stab in the dark.
I urged the minister, "go ahead". The minister responded:
I cannot say, Mr. Chairman, because it would relate to the oil flow of the consortium and their supplies, both national and international.
I asked:
So the department does not even have a guess?
The minister responded:
Well, Mr. Chairman, it gets into the whole matter of companies and their own contracts. That makes it very difficult for an energy minister to try to assert himself at this stage.
A half a year before, appearing in the Senate energy committee where there are only Liberals and Conservatives, where there is a comfortable muzzling of anything that may be raised, the chairman of that committee, a senator from Calgary, asked the minister: "I would like to return to Hibernia for a moment and a question prompted by Mr. Hopper's testimony to the effect that if Hibernia crude comes onstream it will probably move to the United States". The minister responded: "There is no question about probably, Mr. Chairman, it will move to the U.S."
It must be a terrible thing to be a minister of the Crown, to have what was certainty in December change to the ineffable, the indefinable, the airy and ethereal, by June. That is what happened here, or perhaps it was the change in altitude between the committee room, being a room in the Senate, and the committee meeting room in the House. But regardless of what it was, straightforward answers, answers with some kind of relation to reality, were not to be had, at least not by me in the committee.



We now move to the more grotesque elements of suppression of information here. In this very House yesterday, when a motion taking at face value the assertions of those who hold that this project will be a virtual economic second coming for the people of Newfoundland and for many others across Canada as well, that this will result in a level of prosperity and employment that will just leave everybody leaping up and down with joy, taking all that at face value, the hon. member for Kamloops, the House leader of the New Democratic Party, proposed an amendment at report stage which would simply ask that once a year somebody in government put together a detailed presentation on how wonderful it had become.
We asked in this motion that a report be presented annually to the House indicating (a) the net direct and indirect economic benefits in each Canadian province which results from the Hibernia development project; (b) the net employment benefits in each Canadian province which results from the Hibernia development project, including an analysis of job classifications and salary levels; and (c) the quantities and percentages of oil production which are exported in unrefined or semi-refined states from the project site. That was it in its entirety. It was just a request to see at annual intervals how swell the whole thing had become. You know what happened? Every single member of the Conservative and Liberal caucuses present rose in their places to vote against it, including the hon. member who just took up half a day singing the praises of the project.
These folk are willing to have us buy a pig in a poke. They are willing to have us take a flyer on this project, but they are not willing to let the people of Canada see how it works out over time. What are they afraid of? What are they hiding? What is it in these wonderful predictions that they fear will not be borne out? Could it be that these full time 1,100 jobs, for example, that we are going to wind up with at the end of the project are not going to be found in Newfoundland or even in Canada but, in fact, may be found in the majority in the offices of Mobil in the United States? We do not know. In the absence of any willingness by the Conservatives or the Liberals to engage in any kind of long-term disclosure, I must confess I got me some doubts.
Government Orders
There is another matter here, getting back again to the financing of the project. It is not just the $1,040 million that we will give to this project, which I would like every Canadian citizen to know, is $40 for every man, woman and child in this country. Forty dollars a head, straight to Hibernia in a gift. The people of Canada can amuse themselves thinking about that when they start paying the GST in January. They can think that first $40 of GST they paid-it will take $570 worth of purchases to do it-that first $40 of GST they paid: bang, off to Hibernia. If we roll in the loan guarantees and the loans as well, that is another $2,135 billion. That is $82 per capita. Eighty two bucks in GST. That is $1,170 worth of purchases in the new year on which the GST is paid, bang, off to Hibernia. That is just in the legislation authorizing the $1.4 billion contribution.
There is as well the matter before the House now of the privatization of Petro-Canada. Part of this privatization scheme is to take the first 15 per cent share offering and plough all that money right back into the company. Market analysts who know a lot more about this than I do have been quoted publicly as saying that that is going to generate somewhere around $500 million to $700 million for Petro-Canada. Do you know what the value of Petro-Canada's participation in Hibernia is, Mr. Speaker? It is somewhere between $500 million and $700 million. That is what their equity share will amount to. That means, given that the public purse is being ripped off for this 15 per cent share that is going to be ploughed back into this heroically privatized Petro-Canada, the people of Canada are in fact going to wind up footing a bill of somewhere between $1.5 billion and $1.7 billion. Free money to Hibernia. Not to put too fine an edge on it, this is nuts. This is bizarre.
When I came to the House less than two years ago, I never thought I would see the day when these Conservatives-who keep proclaiming their undying fealty to the free market, their unalloyed devotion to the market red in tooth and claw-propose that the Canadian taxpayer with a smile on her or his lips just give $1.5 billion so that Mobil Oil can ship oil out of the Atlantic Ocean down to the northeast United States. This defies credulity, but it seems to be the case. It is odd, it is bizarre, but it is the

Government Orders
case. It is why again I say, and again I note, that our caucus cannot in conscience support this bill.
I am astonished that the Liberals can put themselves through whatever contortions are required in order to do so. I have lost my capacity to be astounded at the actions of the government, however.
In conclusion, there are merits to the Hibernia project. These are merits that the NDP has recognized for a long time. These are merits that the NDP would like to see developed further, but not at any price and not as the consequence of a ludicrous deal struck by some irresponsible federal government with the sharpies of the private sector oil industry. Mr. Speaker, they was took and we ain't gonna to be a party to their being took.

Mr. Speaker, in the two minutes that I have, I want to sum up, if I may, having spoken twice in the last week on this question.

The second question, therefore, is how do we-as Canadians, as governments, as industries, as people who provide jobs, create wealth and create commerce in this country-accommodate that?
Then, we must ask, is it possible that the needs and the interests of all the parties can be met in designing a project that will lead to other projects and to the creation of these jobs and this wealth?
Over the last number of years the Newfoundland government, the Government of Canada, the oil and gas companies that have the knowledge, the capability, and the industrial capacity to develop this project, have come together in the interests of those parties individually, but also in the interests of all Canadians.

As we move from this day to the development of this project into production; as we see other projects develop and move into production; as we see jobs created; as we see Canadians across the country work to contribute to this project, the financial commitment of the government and the people of Canada will have been worth while. PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT TREATMENT AND DISCHARGE OF WASTE WATERS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with municipal, regional, towardand provincial governments in establishing a cost-shared

October 4, 1990
Private Members' Business
program toward the implementation of innovative programs for the treatment and discharge of domestic and industrial waste waters, which programs would include alternative methods of land-based disposal.
He said: Madam Speaker, I would like you, for a moment, to imagine that you are on vacation in Quebec and you are strolling along the banks of the St. Lawrence River, enjoying the beauty of the oncoming fall colours and the peaceful respite of your solitude with nature. Suddenly, along the water's edge approaches no fewer than 15,000 garbage trucks. You are, naturally, mystified by the procession and horrified as each truck pulls up to the edge of the river bank and proceeds to dump its foul contents into the swirling waters. Naturally, as anyone would be, you are outraged. You rush to alert the authorities about the environmental horror and are even more shocked when you are politely told that this is in fact nothing unusual, that it happens every day.
Preposterous, you say. Well, quite the contrary, because although it does not happen in such an obvious manner, the fact is that these 15,000 garbage trucks represent the equivalent of the 500 million litres of untreated waste water and the 50 metric tons of raw sewage that are dumped into the St. Lawrence River every day of the year, and it represents the kind of despoliation that occurs daily across this country of ours, pollution that occurs because from Victoria to St. John's, our Canadian towns and municipalities are struggling with outdated and inadequate sewage treatment and waste management facilities.
A while back, some towns along the Ottawa River had to close beaches to swimming because the heavy rains had overwhelmed the municipal sewage treatment facilities. Out west, where six pulp mills along the Fraser River dump an estimated 32,000 tonnes of toxic waste into the river every year, environmental organizations have now labelled the Fraser the biggest open sewer line in British Columbia. In some areas, such as Newcastle, New Brunswick, creeping groundwater pollution from industrial leakage has contaminated the city water supply to the point that residents of that town have to rely on delivery trucks to supply bottled water, at a cost of some $32,000 each week.
There is a danger in our water. There is a danger in our lakes and our river systems that support our wildlife and our fisheries, and a danger to the Canadian people who must consume this resource. It is a danger that we,
as Canadians, are only now becoming aware of. Many Canadians today do not believe the assurances that Canada's tap water is safe to drink. According to a Gallup poll published last October, some 95 per cent of Canadians are concerned about the health quality of their drinking water, water that often must be treated extensively to remove sewage contaminants before actually being consumed. The fact is, we have been reckless. We have been reckless about the judicious husbandry of an invaluable resource in this country, a resource we have taken for granted because as everyone, including our envious neighbours to the south believe, Canada has oodles of water. But, does it? Despite the fact that Canada holds some 20 per cent of the world's freshwater supplies, only 9 per cent of that is available for our use. The rest is termed fossil water, a legacy of the last ice age, and that 9 per cent is a resource at risk.
As well, over 60 per cent of our rivers flow northward where only 10 per cent of Canada's population lives. Major sections of our population throughout the prairies and the interior dry belt of British Columbia live in areas of chronic water shortage and must rely on groundwater supplies that are becoming increasingly contaminated.
Canadians have, largely out of ignorance, squandered their water resources. Canadians on a per capita basis are the world's second largest consumer of freshwater. We squander some 4,100 litres of water each day for every man, woman and child in this country. For too long water in Canada has been treated as a free commodity with no incentive for conservation. It is estimated that it takes some 5,000 litres of water just to put a restaurant meal on the table. The average Canadian uses about 500 litres of water each day, although his or her biological needs are only about one or two litres a day. Think about this. It takes over 10,000 litres of water to raise half a pound of beef. When considering evaporation from irrigation, it requires some 1,500 litres of fresh water every day to nourish a single apple tree growing in the Okanagan Valley.
Evidence of our over-exploitation of fresh water resources is all around us. Experts have been warning us for years. We need to curb the wasteful use of fresh water supplies. We need to develop the appropriate methods to replenish our waste waters and we need to reduce the outrageous dumping of industrial and domestic wastes into our rivers and lakes.
October 4, 1990

Our groundwater reservoirs, or aquifers as they called, are increasingly polluted by pesticides, agricultural chemicals, runoff from domestic and industrial dumps, leakage from underground gasoline, oil and septic tanks. In our lakes and rivers, pollution from human activities has destroyed aquatic life, is inhibiting the reproductive capacity of mammals and birds and now seriously threatens the health of Canadian citizens. Such pollution has seriously disturbed the composition of wildlife species and has increased the rate of species extinction in Canada. It is estimated that aquatic ecosystems in some parts of North America have lost up to 20 per cent of their indigenous species because of acidification of our lakes.
Estimates of the number of lakes at risk in Canada from pollution of airborne contaminants range up to 600,000. Already as many as 100,000 lakes have been seriously damaged. Another 14,000 are biologically dead. Over 360 chemical compounds have been found in our Great Lakes. Among them are a number of persistent toxins which due to biomagnification and concentration build up in our food pyramid and affect those animal species at the top of the pyramid, including man.
Alkylated lead, benzopyrene, ethylenediamine tetra acetate, hexachlorobenzene, polychlorinated biphenyls, dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, words which are a mouthful in themselves, aromatic hydrocarbons with exotic names and a deadly reputation.
Industrial polluters annually discharge over 7.8 billion litres of liquid waste into Canadian lakes and rivers, an amount that is equal to the water that flows over the Niagara Falls in one 10-hour interval. It is no wonder that of the 10 most highly valued species of fish in Lake Ontario, seven have almost completely disappeared. It is no wonder that of the species still remaining, tumours and cancerous lesions have been found in their tissues. It is no wonder that the beluga whale, the friendly giants, as they call them, of the St. Lawrence have dwindled from a population of over 5,000 at the turn of the century to only 500 today. For the embattled beluga, the victims of deadly toxins spewing out of municipal and industrial waste sites, the St. Lawrence has become a war zone, a war in which the ultimate victim is man himself.
Private Members' Business
I could go on citing specific instances of serious pollution over Canada's waters from one coast to the other, but I think my point has been made perhaps alarmingly clear. The fact is that we can no longer use our waterways as convenient repositories for our wastes. To allow our mighty rivers, the St. Lawrence, the Fraser, the Columbia, the Saskatchewan, the Ottawa, to become nothing more than open sewers is to squander the trust that has been bestowed upon us as the caretakers of this great land.
To continue along our present path jeopardizes the integrity of our environment and with it our economic well-being. In fact, what is at stake here is our very survival. Yet, despite this impending reality Canadian governments, including this government, have been notoriously slow to respond.
The Ontario government's environmental ministry-I speak of the former government-showed that half of the province's industries and one-third of its municipal treatment plants violated water pollution guidelines in 1988.
The Quebec Chamber of Commerce recently commented, an astounding comment, that the provincial government would never close down an industry if it is going to cost jobs, no matter how badly it is harming the environment.
In British Columbia, the Vancouver Sun reported that many of B.C.'s pulp mills would face criminal prosecution if federal guidelines were simply enforced. In fact, it was recently exposed that senior officials and those above, as the quote says, in the federal ministry of fisheries actually blocked legal action against major industrial polluters in the pulp mill industry in B.C. That is an absolutely scandalous situation.
In many parts of Canada municipalities unable to afford the cost of upgrading their sewage treatment facilities continue to contribute knowingly, but what choice have they, to water pollution by dumping untreated or partially treated sewage into the lakes and into the surrounding streams.
In Quebec only 250 of the provinces 1,500 municipalities actually have sewage treatment plants. I think that is about 16 per cent, but it represents only about 6 per cent

October 4, 1990
Private Members' Business
of the province's population. Less than half of Montreal's sewage is treated. The rest is dumped, millions of gallons a day of raw sewage, into the St. Lawrence.
In Ontario, about one-third of the province's municipalities dump partially treated but substandard sewage into its lakes and rivers.
In Newfoundland, more than 48,000 households simply cannot afford and do not have adequate water and sewer service.
The Pearce report of 1985, entitled Currents of Change, calculated that on a national average, only 57 per cent of Canada's population is in fact served by sewage treatment plants. This compares with some 74 per cent of the American population that is serviced by sewage treatment and 99 per cent of the Swedish population who are also served by treatment facilities. So we are well behind the ballgame.
That report became the basis for this federal government's 1987 federal water policy, a policy which has been referred to in the government's often touted green plan, but a document like The Green Plan has remained a toothless statement of philosophical objectives with essentially no legislation to back it up.
However, the federal water policy does commit the government to co-operative approaches with respect to water management with the provinces who, under the provisions of the federal Constitution, exercise direct control over our water resources.
The policy states: "The federal government intends to work with the provinces and territories to encourage safe and sufficient supplies of fresh water" and to "encourage the use of fresh water in an efficient and equitable manner consistent with social, cultural, and environmental needs."
The policy also talks about protecting and enhancing the quality of Canada's waters. Also, it talks about promoting co-operative federal and provincial endeavours, as well as undertaking and supporting research and development in these issues. It also emphasizes the need for an integrated approach to water management.
A reasonable person could only interpret these comments as a commitment from the government, this administration, to become directly involved with water management in co-operation with other levels of government. This is what it says right there in the federal water policy. That commitment, I submit, although it may be well-intentioned, has never been realized.
I think it is time that the government replaced rhetoric with action. Consultants' studies, policy statements, and green plan documents-these must be supplanted with legislative commitments from the government that will take firm action on Canada's threatened water resources.
That is why my colleagues and I urge the Minister of the Environment to consider specific legislative initiatives that will allow the federal government to develop cost-shared programs for the implementation of innovative projects for the treatment and discharge of municipal and industrial waste waters.
Further, I would urge that these programs incorporate opportunities for the investigation and the experimentation of alternative methods of sewage disposal, such as land based sewage alternatives.
I have heard the arguments that, because water resources are a provincial concern, really the solutions should be left to the provinces. But I reiterate that the government's own stated policy is to work co-operatively with other governments with respect to our inland waters. When it comes right down to it, the pollution of one of our most precious resources should be everyone's concern.
I have made a lot of statements critical about the health of Canada's water resources, so I would like to point out that there are also some real success stories in the country.
For example, the communities of Vernon and Osoyoos in the Okanagan Valley have demonstrated what can be accomplished when a community sets its mind to the task of cleaning up its own back yard. These two communities-one in the north end of the valley and one in the south end of the valley-have put their sewage to work for them. They have been disposing of it as treated waste water on surrounding grasslands and crops. In so doing, they have actually helped keep the sewage out of the interior lakes and have aided in the restoration of the quality of the waters of those lakes.
I want to add at this point that the town of Vernon is now attempting to expand its spray irrigation program where the treated effluent is sprayed on the surrounding
October 4, 1990

agricultural land. It wants to expand that by implementing a pilot project for what it terms wildland irrigation. In this concept, treated effluent is applied to the wildlands such as forest crops. In the case of Vernon, the wildland crop is poplar trees. The nutrients are taken up by the trees, enhance the growth of the trees, and can actually be put to a commercial use.
I want to submit that these kinds of innovative efforts take money. They take more money than our financially strapped communities across Canada can afford. Often, they take more money than provinces can afford.
Many worthwhile projects for sewage treatment sit idle because the cost is too great for these smaller players to go it alone. That is why I submit that the federal government has to lend a helping hand to the communities, as well as to the provinces, in addressing this long-term and increasingly difficult problem. Cost-shared programs between municipal, provincial, and federal authorities to clean up Canada's waters are needed and have actually been sought for some time. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities warns that throughout Canada public health and safety, as well as economic development, are at risk because basic investments have not been made in the needed facilities.
In closing, I would like to say that the government has a unique opportunity to demonstrate its commitment to water quality through a number of initiatives. For example the community of Vernon, working with a local environmental society called the Save our Lakes, or SOL, society has made application for federal funding for their wildland irrigation project that I just talked about. Through this project, the town of Vernon and the community could well pave the way for the development throughout Canada of an innovative and commercially viable means of removing sewage from our lakes and our rivers.
The application for the project was made through the newly created Environmental Partners Fund and to date it has fallen only on deaf ears by the government. I appeal to the Minister of the Environment to seize the initiative by funding worthwhile projects such as Vernon's wildland irrigation schemes. Put your commitment on the line by funding these co-operative ventures.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap for his very illuminating address and his very sincere expression of interest in a major problem, a major area of concern to all Canadians.
I would like to address his subject from a different point of view and to talk a little bit about who pays. Obviously, all members in the House would support the objective to provide Canadians with safe clean water for drinking and for other uses. However, the underlying thrust of the motion seems to be aimed at drawing the federal government back into direct subsidies of municipal infrastructure.
I am pleased to say that I had the experience some years ago of acting as Mayor of Fredericton and as president of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, participating and co-chairing the last tri-level conference of government in the country. We made a very serious effort at some formal structure to bring federal financing directly into the municipal stream through and around the provinces. We were not very successful. It was a very, I would say, aggressive effort by provincial governments to insist that municipalities were creatures of the provinces and therefore any aid to come from the federal government should go to the provinces and be distributed by them to the municipalities, and that the federal government should, in effect, keep its hands off direct municipal intervention. To some extent, I think that that remains true today.
The question of who should pay for municipal infrastructure was also debated, as many members will recall, at great length throughout the 1980s. To a large extent, the real questions being debated today is who will face the unpopular task of coaxing more dollars out of the taxpayers' pockets and who will do the more popular job of spending it.
There are three viewpoints which dominate that debate. The first group, not exclusively but primarily at the municipal level, paints legitimate horror stories about the state of our water supplies and sewage systems. They are emphatic that the job is just too big financially for municipalities to handle. They say that senior government must provide hefty subsidies and besides, they say,

October 4, 1990
Private Members' Business
the senior government will get it all back through fiscal recapture and it will, in addition, solve our unemployment problems in the process.
Critics of this group did not deny that municipalities were struggling with very real problems in municipal finance, particularly as their ratepayers demanded higher levels and more elaborate levels of service. However, they questioned the logic of municipalities and their taxpayers subsidizing each other through federal and provincial coffers. They also questioned whether the fiscal recapture was real or largely illusory.
The second group-let us call them constitutional purists-generally supported these criticisms. However, they went somewhat further. They pointed to the Constitution as giving one role to the federal government and another, for matters of local concern, to the provinces. They pointed to the hefty level of transfer payments already made to the provinces and to the huge deficit and debt service charges at the federal level, about which we debate in the House almost every day.
They questioned whether federal dollars would be regarded as found money with equivalent amounts being transferred to more glamorous municipal projects and very little being done over all toward putting water and sewer systems on a sound financial footing, ensuring technological improvement, or effecting conservation of water in quality and quantity terms.
Surprisingly, the constitutional purists' group was not found totally at the federal level. Provinces frequently reminded the federal government that municipalities are their business. That was their line back in 1974 when I was last involved in this debate. Ottawa may help to provide the money, but the provinces feel that the priority, distribution of funding, and the standards by which it is distributed are their prerogatives. This sentiment also found some expression at the municipal level. Municipalities, such as Fredericton where I reside, which had provided their own residents with a high level of services, objected to the prospect of contributing to the needs of other municipalities, both within and outside their provinces, that have not yet dealt with those problems.
These debates have been useful. Although very little has been resolved, at least two things have been accomplished. First, the financial needs camp has established in the minds of the citizenry the harsh reality that we have not done a very good job in handling municipal infrastructures. Second, the constitutional purists' camp has forced us to consider who is responsible and who is in the best position to effect over-all changes in our approach to municipal infrastructure.
The third view, and it is not necessarily new, but it is gaining rapid acceptance in water management circles, not just in Canada but all over the world. This group, which is supported by this government, claims that if the user pays most of the cost directly, we will not only get the least cost solution but we also get other other water management and environmental advantages.
The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, OECD, published a major study on the pricing of water services a few months ago. It found that the extent of subsidization of water services varied greatly within and across OECD countries, but was generally higher in the OECD's off-centre members in North America, Japan and Australia. The report strongly supported the general applicability of the user-pay principle. The essential element of that principle is that an incentive is provided for the user to economize in the use of the service of natural resources. Users of the service would in aggregate pay the full cost of the provision of the service and a charging system would share out these costs among users.
This is similar to, and indeed embraces, the more familiar polluter-pays principle, where the polluter pays for the cost which his pollution imposes on society. Under the user-pay principle, the OECD argues that subsidization by taxpayers and cross-subsidization among water service users should be abolished unless special social reasons exist for their retention.
As most hon. members are no doubt aware, the federal government supported these principles in its November, 1987, federal water policy. Since nobody likes to be characterized as unreasonable or rigid, we also hear a lot of variations and combinations of the three themes. The most common one is, yes, we accept that the real and lasting solution is full-cost pricing, but the country has
October 4, 1990

such a backlog that we should revert to the subsidy route for a few years until we catch up.
Another qualification which nobody really disputes is that there has to be some financial redistribution role played by senior governments. For example, through federal transfer payments and provincial assistance to smaller communities.
I would like to touch very briefly on the temporary subsidy for catch-up question. These are some of the problems I see with senior government bridge funding.
First, the municipalities which would be able to take advantage of such funding would be those which are planning to undertake the work anyway in the near future.
Second, eligible projects and costs would have to be determined by some government agency or agencies. The rules under the CMHC program became very complicated and where they were regarded by the province as excessive federal red tape, they were not used and eventually the program was withdrawn entirely.
Third, having restored the subsidy program, there would be inevitable pressures to extend it. The initial forgiveness feature of the CMHC program was only to last two or three years. In fact, through extension, it lasted 18 years.
Finally, and most important, a bridge funding program would be counterproductive in the sense that it would simply delay movement towards a more rational longterm solution.
In closing, I would like to quote from a speech which Harvard University's Peter Rodgers delivered to a Science Council of Canada workshop recently.
In the area of the water resources we should remember that we
get exactly what we pay for. In both Canada and the United States,
the prices charged for water are so low as to be not believable.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap said the same thing in his address.
We deliver a valuable commodity to very wealthy consumers who would be willing to pay substantial amounts for it. He suggests that by combining an aggressive pricing policy with tough, environmental laws, it will enable Canada to get control of its water resources in a way that will be efficient from the point of view of

the market and the environment. Everybody will be better off.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to start by congratulating the hon. member for the NDP on his speech. It is encouraging to hear a member of the New Democratic Party in this House speak so positively about improving infrastructures in this country.

Mr. Speaker, as you will recall in the 1988 election, when this issue was raised by the Leader of the Opposition at the time, Mr. John Turner, the NDP refused to back up any kind of a plan or any kind of a thorough initiative when it came to infrastructure.
I am quite encouraged now to see that there is some sort of a policy or attitude change. That is very encouraging for the simple reason that as we in the Liberal Party have always called on all members of the House regardless of their political background, to support a federal initiative that will involve a partnership with the provinces, as well as the municipalities.
If you recall, Mr. Speaker, we had promised $5 billion towards infrastructure in Canada. In our rationale at the time, $5 billion over five years, would put us in a position to create approximately 314,000 jobs. Jobs are very much needed across the land. At the time, we used the rationale which was proposed by Informetrica, a consultant company, who stated that it was three times the number of jobs that would have been created by the then free trade agreement.
My colleague, representing the government side, have used some historical argument in order to back some of the statements he was making. He gave, in my view, a philosophical answer to a real problem. I would like to remind him that participation in municipal infrastructure goes back to between 1938 and 1949, when the Municipal Improvement Assistance Act was in place. The federal government then gave money towards roads, water and sewerage.
Then we had another program which was called the Sewage Treatment Program that was established in 1961 and went on to 1974. In 1963 to 1966, we had a Municipal Development and Loans Act which put a system into

October 4, 1990
Private Members' Business
place to help municipalities deal with issues of sewage as well as transportation systems.
In 1973 to 1979 the Neighbourhood Improvement Program was put in place with the objective to bring in funding for sewer, water distribution systems, parks and other related issues.
In 1975 to 1978 the Municipal Infrastructure Program was put in place to introduce grants for pollution, sewage treatment, land development. At that time, over $1 billion was granted in terms of loans and $395 million was given in terms of grants.
In 1979 the Community Service Contribution Program was put in place with the objective also to help municipalities deal with the issue of sewer and water projects, social and recreational programs. At the time we had put in place $221 million in grants, with the final disbursement which took place in 1984. At that time, the government which the hon. member represents ended the program and we have not seen any funding coming through since that time.
On Friday, May 25, 1990 I introduced a motion in this House, on behalf of our party, and I would just like to read it for the hon. member of the NDP so he can just recall what was said then. The motions reads:
That this House call upon the government to recognize that Canada's municipal infrastructure is facing a crisis of national proportions and that, given the serious implications to the nation's environment, economic prosperity and quality of life for Canadians, the government resume its traditional role as a partner with the provincial and municipal governments to address this national crisis.
We said that then, and we are saying the same thing again. For the Liberal Party and our caucus, the issue of infrastructure, sewage and waterways is important. We have launched a national task force to go across the land. For us it was a priority, it remains a priority and will always continue to be a priority. We have launched a task force where every single member of our caucus has participated in its deliberations and have encouraged groups in the municipalities within their ridings to come forward and make presentations. I would like to indicate that our task force had the total support of the board of management of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. For the information of the House and those who are watching, I would like to outline some of the recommendations the Liberal Party of Canada made as early as May 25, 1990.
We believe that there is no single action that will be enough to ensure the future health and viability of Canada's infrastructure. We believe that a broad range of measures is necessary to make a meaningful difference, specifically, those should include the following.
First, we want to see a federal recognition of municipal infrastructure as a crisis of national proportions. We want to see a federal commitment to share the responsibility for municipal infrastructure with its provincial and municipal counterparts. We want to see the establishment of minimum national criteria for infrastructure to provide environmental protection and uniform levels of service for all Canadians.
The Liberal Party would like to see a federal commitment to rehabilitate and expand the Trans-Canada Highway. The Liberal party supports the establishment of a process through which the federal government can take actions which include: clarifying the respective roles of federal, provincial and municipal governments in infrastructure construction and management. That would respond to some of the concerns my colleague was talking about a little earlier.
Also, the Liberal Party spoke about identifying and prioritizing needs on a national scale in consultation with, and with the concurrence of provincial and municipal governments. The Liberal Party also called for increased incentives for maintenance and reconstruction of existing capital assets and the use of low capital environmentally conscious techniques, such as waste reduction and recycling.
We spoke about exploring alternative funding sources, such options as rational user fees, as my colleague has indicated, for water services, applying fuel tax revenues to road construction and maintenance, and increased private sector involvement. Of course, we collect the taxes on oil, on fuel, but the money which comes through those taxes does not go toward specific projects such as road and sewer systems but, rather, it goes toward general revenues.
We also spoke about the increasing support for research and development to accelerate technological innovation. Finally, we are encouraging efficient municipal management methods to permit phased programs of rehabilitation and better management of infrastructure systems and effective use of funds.

These are some of the recommendations with which our task force has come forward. Of course, we in the Liberal Party do not have to be reminded about the crisis and the fact that it is reaching national proportions, because we were there. We were in Atlantic Canada. We were in Newfoundland, where 48,000 homes have inadequate water and sewer services and 80 per cent of the residents do not have properly treated drinking water.
In Nova Scotia, in the municipalities of Sydney and Halifax, sewage systems just simply do not exist, so we have to set up and put new systems in place.
P.E.I. is an excellent example again, where the problem there is out of proportion.
I want to cite this. In Quebec, 500 million litres of untreated water and 50 tonnes of raw sewage are dumped into the St. Lawrence River every day. That is incredible.
Of course I would appreciate it if my colleague in the NDP could speak to his colleagues, so at least we can in this House and Canadians can find out where the NDP are coming from, whether they have a heart or not and whether they do support the Liberal initiative or they do support a federal involvement on the issue of infrastructure. Having said all of this, I commend the hon. member. Of course, his heart is in the right place.

Mr. Speaker, although Bill C-72, the new Official Languages Act, was passed by this Parliament almost unanimously on September 12, 1988, more than two years ago, and it was fully supported I might say at that time by the Liberal Party, that bill still remains inoperative because the government which presented the bill has failed to produce the regulations.
I want to point out that the content of that bill, a great improvement in our official languages legislation, had been discussed at great length for several years by the Joint Standing Committee on Official Languages of
which I was a member and which committee, representing all parties in this House and the Senate, made recommendations for the reform and improvement of the Official Languages Act.
Finally the government took up those recommendations, put them into Bill C-72-and I congratulate them for it-presented the bill, and it passed. But, as I say, despite its passage and great words which were stated in favour of the bill at that time, it remains inoperative because the government has failed to produce the regulations. As a result of not producing the regulations the bill for the most part remains inoperative.
I must point out that when the bill was before the House the minister responsible for the bill, in answer to questions, said that the regulations would be produced shortly afterward. Then, in answer to questions in the House, that promise was repeated in August 1989 when the minister said that the regulations would be produced before the end of 1989. Then again last April 4, when the Commissioner of Official Languages tabled his annual report and condemned the government for not producing the regulations, and even threatened to resign, the minister said that the regulations would be presented soon after June 23 of this year. Here we are in October and we still do not have those regulations.
I would like to refer to what the Prime Minister said when we were debating Bill C-72. He suggested two and a half years ago when the Official Languages Act was being debated that the House would have to sit every day of the week, if necessary, to pass the legislation that was owed to the Canadian population. The people of Canada deserve now to see that legislation implemented; the usual politics of rhetoric by the Prime Minister. He was at that time saying that we would have to sit day and night to pass the legislation, which we did. I think the only ones who voted against it were a few members of his own party, and here we are more than two years later without the regulations to implement the bill.
Again we have had, just this past June 14, the joint standing committee pass the resolution unanimously with Conservatives, Liberals, New Democrats, senators all agreeing and saying that the government should introduce those regulations as soon as possible. That was in June. Still no action, Mr. Speaker.
While the government has failed to act in this matter, tensions have continued to grow between the language
October 4, 1990

groups in this country. We had the failure of the Meech Accord which produced tension. The passage of Bill 178 in Quebec; the growth of APEC, the Association for the Protection of English in Canada, which is really a very prejudiced and bigoted group against the francophones of this country; the passage of resolutions by the Ontario municipalities for unilingualism; the rise of the Reform Party here in this Parliament and the Bloc Quebecois; all gravitating against justice and understanding for both language groups in Canada and showing a great need for this improved legislation, legislation which is government legislation.

Mr. Speaker, discrimination is against the law in Canada. It is against the law in Canada to discriminate in many different ways: by way of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status, family status, pardoned conviction, or disability.
On May 30 I asked a question in the House about discrimination at the CRTC, Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission. The government's answer, which I will get to shortly, was totally unsatisfactory. The basic elements of the case are that

October 4, 1990
Adjournment Debate
the Canadian Human Rights Commission had found the CRTC guilty of discrimination. The CRTC refused to arrive at a settlement in the case, for example it refused to admit wrongdoing. The CRTC refused to accept conciliation or at least refused to come to agreement at conciliation, thus forcing the employee to go to a tribunal, the next stage.
At the tribunal the CRTC, acting in typical management style, gave notice that no matter which way the tribunal proceeded it would appeal to the courts.
In this particular case there was an out of court settlement agreed to by the employee after more hassling than most people could bear and which I do not have the time to describe.
However, the bottom line is that-wonder of wonders-there is no record of discrimination at the CRTC. Is that not wonderful? That is only half the story. The other half is even worse. The employee who originally filed was harassed for having taken the action, which in itself is against the law, but other employees were harassed even more severely for giving evidence on behalf of the complainant.
Section 59 of the Human Rights Act provides for fines up to $50,000 for threatening, intimidating or discriminating against an individual who has filed a complaint, or for hampering the investigation process.
An RCMP investigation under section 59 of the Human Rights Act determined that by harassing those who supported the original employee who complained there were grounds for laying criminal charges against the management of the CRTC.
There is a catch. Section 60(4) provides that the prosecution cannot be instituted except by the consent of the Attorney General of Canada. That consent was withheld in this human rights case at the CRTC. Except for the discretionary powers of the Attorney General, charges could have been laid against management at the CRTC.
The government argued in response-I am getting to the response of the government at the time I asked the
question on April 30-and I suspect will argue momentarily again that the CRTC is an arm's length organization and the government cannot get involved.
The employees of the CRTC are government employees. I would not want the CRTC to get involved in the day-to-day operations and the day-to-day decisions of whether or not they are going to provide a licence or withhold a licence. By God, I would expect the CRTC first of all-and in this case secondly-or at least the government to be protecting its own employees.
The government had doggone well better get involved in this case, arm's length or not. It certainly is not arm's length. These are government employees. Or else, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Human Rights Act means nothing at all.
If the discretionary powers of the Attorney General can thwart the investigations and decisions of the RCMP and the Human Rights Commission, those discretionary powers have to be removed. There is no justice if a bureaucratic management of the CRTC or a government department can hassle any individual into quitting, into ill health, or an out of court settlement which is not as satisfactory but which gets management off one's back.
I wrote to the Minister of Justice on June 1 asking why the discretionary powers of the Attorney General were allowed to be exercised in that case. So far I have only an acknowledgement of a letter received; no explanation.
More recently speaking, which rather demonstrates the government's commitment to human rights in Canada and for Canadian citizens, I would suggest, at the dinner in celebration of the Canadian tribute to human rights, Lawrence Court d'Oreille, Vice-Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, said: "I am afraid for my human rights in Canada because those who are supposed to be protecting my human rights cannot protect their own."
This government, through its actions in the CRTC case-and who knows how many others-has signalled departments, agencies, Crowns and companies within its jurisdiction that they can discriminate against Canadians and the government will not allow prosecution.
October 4, 1990

Adjournment Debate
Quite simply put, this is an outrage and we cannot allow it to be continued. I call for a public inquiry into the discretionary attitude of the government.
I also call, Mr. Speaker, more principally for a public inquiry into the discriminatory management of the CRTC, hoping thereby that the actions of that kind of management in those kinds of situations may be prevented in the future.
