speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should wish to congratulate you on your recent nomination as Assistant Deputy Chairman of the committees of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, the question raised by the member for Saskatoon-Dundurn relates to three cases dealing with employee-employer relations within an independent regulatory agency, the CRTC, and which are or have been under investigation-I am trying to be helping to the hon. member-by another independent tribunal, the Canadian Human Rights Commission.
To the extent that these cases, two of which are yet unresolved, are of a personal nature, and to the extent that this government respects the independence of its arms length agencies, it would be inappropriate to enter into the details surrounding them, and I will refrain from doing so.
Instead, I will address my comments to the more general issue raised by the member for Saskatoon- Dundurn when he first raised this question on May 30, 1990.
In his question, and his supplementary comments, the member suggested that the CRTC was "forcing its employees to extreme lengths in order to seek basic justice".
It further suggested that it was "unacceptable for an agency of the government to 'force its employees' to go to a tribunal to settle human rights complaints".

I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that his comments denote a seious lack of comprehension of the role and mandate of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. Furthermore, they give the impression that government agencies such as the CRTC do not have the right to respond to complaints from their employees, whether the complaints are founded or not.
The Canadian society is increasingly diversified, which makes for more complex relations between individuals and institutions, including employer-employee relations. Because of the Charter of Rights and the Human Rights Act, the Canadian people are more aware of their rights and more prone to complain when they believe their rights have been infringed upon.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, no government agency or private company can escape complaint. Besides, a complaint can sometimes be the only way to uncover an injustice and seek redress. I would add that the injustices uncovered are not always due to lack of goodwill.
It is precisely with a view to providing a forum for settling human right complaints that the Canadian Human Rights Commission was established by Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, to suggest that it is unacceptable for the CRTC to respond to complaints lodged by employees before the Human Rights Commission is to deny the important role that the Human Rights Commission was designed to perform. It is no disgrace for any employer to respond to a complaint from an employee where the employer has reason to believe that the complaint is unfounded. Indeed, to not respond in such circumstances is to invite abuse. Moreover, it is no disgrace for an employer to challenge the findings of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. No decision by a tribunal or a court of justice, except for the Supreme Court of Canada, is beyond appeal or challenge.
It is important to remember that allegations arising from human rights complaints must be proven and both parties must be able to present fairly their respective sides of the story.

October 4, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Furthermore, because such complaints often involve the subtleties of interpersonal relations, it can be difficult to determine with accuracy where fault lies or what corrective measures should be taken.
In the end, a disgrace would only occur if an employer refused to co-operate in resolving the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased this afternoon to have an opportunity to put before the House the question which I put to the Minister of Employment and Immigration last spring, in March, concerning the lay-off of over 2,000 employees at the Elliot Lake uranium mines. In fact, 450 have already been laid off at Denison Mines in late July and in late August some 1,800 additional employees were laid off at Rio Algom.
The magnitude of these lay-offs is absolutely mind-boggling for this community. It represents at least 50 per cent of the direct mine-related employment in that community. Unless drastic and determined efforts are made by the two senior levels of government, we face a loss of half of the community. This is an urban community of some 16,000 people.
I asked the minister at that time what actions were going to be taken by the federal government. In fact, some actions have taken place. Industrial adjustment committees and community adjustment committees have been established. The industrial adjustment committee was under the leadership of Harold Kenny for the Denison Mines, under the direction of Roger Taylor for the two Rio Algom mines, and the community adjustment committee was under the direction of Craig Mac-quarrie. In fact, those committees have operated in what I would say is in an exemplary way. They have functioned very well.
The one thing that they require is funding for the community adjustment and industrial adjustment. They need dollars for training. They need dollars for job search. They need dollars for job mobility grants. That has been our main problem all through the summer and fall months, whether we would have enough of these funds.
There is a Community Futures program in the area. In fact, they submitted a budget to the staff of the minister
last April, calling for over a two-year period some $16 million. In fact, it is all happening over the course of one year rather than two years. That is the kind of funding which is required for those industrial and community adjustment committees.
So far we have received some $3 million or $4 million. Unfortunately, that whole budget of $16 million has to be telescoped into one year rather than into two, or slightly more than one year, and the committees have done an excellent job. The problem that we have is the uncertainty. The official budget for the community and industrial adjustment has not ever been approved yet, so we are going along sort of month to month, getting a commitment of $900,000 in July, $1 million in August. That level of adjustment funding I believe will be needed for another six to twelve months, depending on how successful the individuals are in securing employment.
The government of course argues: "We cannot provide the funding for the community and industrial adjustment because Bill C-21 has not been passed". Of course that argument is simply not accepted. Everybody knows that the government has been collecting money under Bill C-21 since last January. In fact, the fees for unemployment insurance have gone up by some 15 per cent collecting, I would guess, over $1 billion this year already, so my miners in Elliot Lake do not buy that argument. If they can collect the money under Bill C-21, then they can spend it under Bill C-21 or they can spend it under supplementary estimates and repay the money from the funding that is being taken from employees day after day.
Mr. Hockin has been designated by the Deputy Prime Minister to be a special liaison officer to work with the communities. He has visited the community, outlined a number of initiatives which the government has agreed to put forward, including providing an additional $1 million of funding in late August. Our concern is that we have this commitment for training and adjustment funds every month until the miners have had an opportunity to seek new employment and are able to get on with then-lives, or retrained for another job.
We need co-operation from the federal government for the initiatives which are being taken by the province which are quite extensive. They include a study on a retirement living program which has been very succes-
October 4, 1990

sful. There are a number of proposals relating to the CANMET lab where it would become a field station associated with Laurentian University. The province has provided funding for a drug and alcohol addiction centre which would follow along from the Camilla Centre operated by the Sisters of St. Joseph.
We have a number of initiatives, but we need a commitment from the federal government that its portion will be funded as well.
This week I have put before the minister a number of proposals for the decentralization of government offices from Toronto and other regions of the country into northern Ontario and Elliot Lake. After all, it is the sixth largest urban centre in northern Ontario. We cannot afford a community with all assets and advantages of this community to die. We must diversify the economy. We must develop what we have. I am pleading and asking the government to do this. I believe the community is working very hard to do that as well. I am asking for the support, encouragement, and assistance of the federal government to carry its fair share in this regard.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, I am pleased to have the opportunity to discuss the initiatives the government has undertaken to help laid- off workers in Elliot Lake.
Our industrial adjustment service consultants have worked closely with Denison Mines, Rio Algom Ltd., and the United Steelworkers Union in the province of Ontario to provide assistance to laid-off workers in Elliot Lake.
For example, two separate industrial adjustment committees were set up to help workers and management deal with the Denison Mines layoff and the Rio Algom closures respectively. Through the industrial adjustment service committee, Employment and Immigration Canada provided $106,000 to help Denison Mines workers and $102,600 to help the Rio Algom workers.
The member should know that of the 420 employees laid off at Denison Mines, 344 have now positive plans for employment or training, and 26 are taking early retirement.
Adjournment Debate
The Department of Employment and Immigration is also providing $114,000, matched by the province of Ontario, to establish a community adjustment centre to help other local workers whose employment could be threatened and disrupted by the lay-offs.
A co-ordinating committee for Elliot Lake was formed to set priorities and determine how training funds available to the area should be spent.
Employment and Immigration approved an $818,000 grant to finance additional activities under the Skills Shortages and Job Development programs of the Canadian Jobs Strategy for relocation, training, and community economic development and adjustment assistance.
In August, 1990, $1 million in additional federal funding was announced in relocation and exploratory assistance to meet needs of the Elliot Lake community.
The hon. gentleman should know that other assistance from the government would have been provided to communities like Elliot Lake, if it had the labour force development strategy implemented and if Bill C-21 were passed.
The member for Algoma knows that many laid-off workers requested relocation assistance or additional funds to start their own businesses because they felt that this was the way to go from now on. The government could have helped these workers if Bill C-21 and the Labour Force Development Strategy were in place. With the Labour Force Development Strategy and Bill C-21, the government intends to raise by $45 million the funding for relocation assistance and self-employment initiatives.
Many people in Elliot Lake also felt that they could take over their own destiny and work out a restructuring plan for Elliot Lake. Elliot Lake is already eligible for help under the Community Futures Program for creation of small businesses and self-employment, for training and other community initiatives. But the government cannot ignore the fact that additional assistance under the Labour Force Development Strategy could have been made available to the people in Elliot Lake if Bill C-21 had been passed by the Senate.
Finally, earlier in this response, the success of the industrial adjustment committee in helping laid-off workers at Denison and Rio Algom was discussed. The government believed that workers would have benefited from a doubling of the industrial adjustment service funds. They did not benefit from this doubling of funds simply because Bill C-21 is still in the Senate and, as a

October 4, 1990

result, the Labour Force Development Strategy is not implemented.
If the hon. member truly wants to assist the people of Elliot Lake, he will reverse his position on Bill C-21, stop voting against his constituents, urge his unelected Liberal associates in the Senate to stop playing politics with peoples' lives, and have them do something useful for a change.
